spectrum.interested: After the store-brand pasta went into the cart, Sam said, "I don't mind splitting month-end grocery runs." Then, without pressing, "Or keep it as is; your call." They left the receipt on the counter, uncircled, and mentioned it again three days later only to say the offer stood if it helped.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday Sam had typed a shared note: who buys milk, who returns the borrowed ladder, who texts before 6 p.m. if plans shift. A neighbor's spare key went back on its hook labelled. Nothing was signed; the note lived on the fridge, and both names appeared as editors. That's checkable.
spectrum.done: On Saturday Sam said plainly, "I'm not hosting every holiday here; I'll do two." The reply: "Understood, I'll ask before assuming." A reader can respect that by not re-asking in a different form, watching what actually changes, and deciding their own limit without treating a slow text as a verdict.

works.detail: Before a hard conversation, decide together who or what settles it. A shared note, a neutral friend, a rule you both wrote. The point is a stated answer you can cite later, not a perfect answer.

works.point: Put the rule where both can see it
works.detail: Write down the arrangement in plain words and keep it somewhere you both can open. A rule held only in one person's memory is easy to revise in their favor without anyone noticing.
When the method you proposed produces a result you dislike, follow it or ask openly to amend it. Quietly abandoning your own process tells the other person the process was never meant for them.
If a change will affect your partner, say what it means for them before you enact it. A decision that lands as a surprise invites a response you did not plan for, and both of you pay for that.
After a decision, ask whether the agreed method actually worked. A short review keeps the arrangement honest and gives either of you a clean way to say this part needs adjusting.

never.point: Never make the rule retroactive
never.detail: Applying a new arrangement to a dispute that already happened, without agreement, reads as a way to win the past. Say plainly when a rule starts and let earlier matters stand as they were.

never.point: Never hide the method until it matters
never.detail: Keeping quiet about how you plan to decide until the stakes are high leaves the other person unable to consent. Name the method while the outcome is still uncertain for both of you.

never.point: Never use a process to isolate
never.detail: A formal arrangement that cuts a partner off from friends or family is not a fair forum. Keep the people who care about you both inside the conversation where you can.

never.point: Never treat a settled matter as a weapon
never.detail: Reopening an agreed decision to punish someone erodes the trust that made the agreement possible. If circumstances changed, say so and propose an amendment openly.

never.point: Never confuse declaration with agreement
never.detail: Saying a matter is resolved does not make it resolved. Check that the other person actually concurs, and ask what they understood, before you treat the question as closed.

power_moves.name: The moving venue
power_moves.how_it_works: They agree to one method of deciding, then switch to another when the first answer looks unfavorable, citing a fresh reason each time. The effect is that you never know which rule you are playing by and start negotiating the rules instead of the issue.
power_moves.defense: Say the method we agreed is the one we use, and if you want a different one, ask me before the next decision. Then hold the agreed document in view and decline to argue inside a venue you did not choose.

power_moves.name: The published fait accompli
power_moves.how_it_works: They announce a change as already decided and final, framing it as necessary and urgent, so that objecting feels like obstruction. The effect is that your response arrives after the costs are locked in, which is how the July 1861 suspension met its creditors.
power_moves.defense: You can say I need notice before a change lands on me, and ask for the date it starts. If it has already started, ask what it means for you in plain terms and decline to treat the announcement as agreement.

power_moves.name: The rule that only points one way
power_moves.how_it_works: The method they propose produces fair results while the numbers favor them and unfair ones when they do not, yet the rule survives only in the first case. The effect is a bar that moves, and over time you stop trusting any method they suggest.
power_moves.defense: Keep a short record of decisions and outcomes for a month. When a rule bends, point to the earlier instance and ask whether it still applies. If it does not, ask directly what would make it apply equally.

power_moves.name: The crisis override
power_moves.how_it_works: They invoke an emergency to bypass an agreed process, and the emergency is real enough that questioning it seems petty. The effect is that every hard moment becomes a mandate for unilateral action, and the shared rule is never tested under pressure.
power_moves.defense: Acknowledge the emergency and still ask what the urgent decision is for you specifically. Offer a narrow, temporary exception with an end date rather than an open-ended permission.

power_moves.name: The manifesto close
power_moves.how_it_works: They declare a matter resolved and speak as though both parties already agree, so that disagreement looks like denial of a known fact. The effect is that you spend energy proving the conversation is unfinished rather than having it.
power_moves.defense: Say I do not remember agreeing to that, and ask what they understood you to have accepted. Restate your own position in one sentence and ask for theirs before anyone calls the matter closed.

leverage.detail: You can propose your own process instead of accepting theirs. Say what would make a decision feel fair to you, such as a deadline, a neutral third person, or a written summary, and ask if they will use it. Watch whether they engage or deflect.

You can require advance notice of changes that affect you. Ask what a decision will cost you before it happens. If notice is refused, that is information about how decisions will be made, and you can weigh it before committing further.

leverage.point: Test mutuality with a small reversal
leverage.detail: Propose a rule that would sometimes favor them and sometimes favor you, such as alternating who picks the weekend plan. Notice whether they accept it when it costs them something, which is a fair test of whether the method is shared or convenient.

A private log of agreements and outcomes is not suspicion, it is a check. If you ever need to point to a promise, you can do it precisely. You can also use the log to catch a pattern early and raise it calmly.

You can say no to a process you do not trust and still stay in the relationship on your terms. State one condition for continuing and one thing you will not accept, then let the other person respond without pressure from you.

closest.rationale: As justice minister, Juárez issued the Ley Juárez, which suppressed the ecclesiastical and military fueros in civil matters, fixing in a published rule which forum would hear such cases instead of leaving it to custom.

cousin.tell: Where a Reframer would restate a stalled argument to open it, Juárez instead fixed the forum in writing: the Ley Juárez assigned civil suits to ordinary courts, converting a standing jurisdictional standoff into an external rule anyone could invoke.

basis.observation: The law drew a line between ordinary civil jurisdiction and the separate church and army courts, so a conflict over which forum heard a case had a stated answer that could be cited and tested in practice.

sections.identity: President Lázaro Cárdenas of Mexico delivered a 1938 national radio address from the National Palace announcing expropriation of foreign oil installations.

matches.why: He announced from the National Palace the expropriation decree, publicly defining the decision on petroleum ownership and the means of enacting it through a formal declaration.

pattern: A decision made quietly and a decision made where others can hear it are different objects. In March 1938 the president used a National Palace address to name the petroleum expropriation as the nation's own, and the decree became something citizens could repeat, dispute and check against what followed. The step had already been settled. The announcement made the settling visible.

Announcing is only half of a two-part habit. In 1936 the president entrusted Juan de Dios Bátiz with organizing the Instituto Politécnico Nacional, then announced the institution's creation himself in his September presidential report. Someone else built and the president said plainly what was being built. The pairing matters. A name attached to a result it did not produce is a hollow signature.

Land in La Laguna became ejidos in October 1936, with cotton as the principal crop. The change was not confined to a signature. Farms, tenure and the working season all shifted together, and the region's daily economy had to absorb the rearrangement. A reform that stops at the announcement leaves the fields exactly as they were.

The Comité de Ayuda a los Niños del Pueblo Español, created in 1937 and presided over by Amalia Solórzano, put roughly five hundred Spanish Civil War evacuees into Mexico, including the Niños de Morelia. The decision could have remained a statement of sympathy. Instead it produced beds, schools and named children. Care measured in arrivals is harder to overstate.

text: Listen for whether a person describes a choice as finished or as merely announced. The 1938 address presented an outcome, not an intention, and listeners could weigh it against what came next. In conversation, someone who tells you what they have arranged differs from someone rehearsing what they might do. Ask which one you are hearing.

Notice who is named. When the Instituto Politécnico Nacional came into being, the organizing was assigned to one man and the announcement came from the president's report. Shared credit spoken plainly is easier to trust than a story where every part was done by the speaker alone. Listen for other names in the account and for how they are treated.
examples: On 18 March 1938, President Lázaro Cárdenas delivered a national radio address from the National Palace announcing the expropriation of foreign oil companies' installations, presenting the decree as reasserting Mexican ownership of petroleum resources.
In October 1936, President Lázaro Cárdenas promoted agrarian distribution in La Laguna, converting farmland there into ejidos, with cotton becoming the principal crop.

In 1937, President Lázaro Cárdenas created the Comité de Ayuda a los Niños del Pueblo Español, presided over by his wife Amalia Solórzano, to aid child evacuees of the Spanish Civil War; Mexico took in about 500 children, including the Niños de Morelia.

In 1936, President Lázaro Cárdenas entrusted Juan de Dios Bátiz with organizing the Instituto Politécnico Nacional, and announced the institution's creation himself in his September 1936 presidential report.

spectrum.interested: A repair bill for a cracked screen sits unpaid while a neutral adjuster’s note says the quote is fair. One of them texts the other: "I can cover half Friday—unless you'd rather take it from here." That wording leaves room: an offer with a stated amount and an explicit exit. It reads as tentative interest, not a claim on the answer.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday the two have settled a split: one transfers a set sum, the other calls the shop and books the slot, and both keep the adjuster’s note in a shared folder. These are checkable acts—money moved, an appointment made, a document kept. Nobody has to infer warmth from a slow reply; the choices stand on their own.
spectrum.done: On Friday one writes: "I'm paying my half only; the rest is yours to handle." That is a stated limit, not a verdict on anyone. The other can honor it by sending the amount without argument, then decide whether to keep sharing costs. Respecting the line means accepting the no and choosing your own next step separately.

works.detail: If you have settled something with a partner, name it in plain words on the same day. What is decided, when it starts, who else knows. An outcome nobody can repeat is not yet shared.

works.point: Name the person doing the work
works.detail: When a partner organizes the trip, hosts the family or handles the difficult call, say so in front of others. Credit given plainly is easy to keep giving and hard to resent.

works.point: Check the fields, not the paperwork
works.detail: After any agreement about money, chores or time, look at the ordinary week. If the split has not changed in practice, the agreement is still a draft. Ask what one concrete thing will look different by Friday.
Support that stays a statement is common. Look for the equivalent of named children and a place to sleep. Ask your partner what actually lands with the person you are both trying to help.
If you announce something jointly, agree beforehand what each of you will say. Mismatched versions travel fast. A five-minute conversation before the call saves a month of correcting.

never.point: Never mistake volume for completion
never.detail: A large announcement can feel like a finished project. It is not. Wait for the first week to pass and check one small thing. If nothing moved, say so without accusation.

never.point: Never sign for someone else's labor
never.detail: If a partner did the organizing, do not retell it as your own initiative. Correct the record in the same conversation. Quiet credit-stealing corrodes faster than open disagreement.

never.point: Never let an announcement replace a plan
never.detail: Telling friends you are moving in together is not a moving date. Keep a written list of the boring steps and review it together every Sunday until the list empties.

never.point: Never confuse sympathy with help
never.detail: Saying you care about a partner's difficult family situation costs nothing. Ask what specific thing would ease this week and offer that. Choose something you can actually deliver.

never.point: Never press for a repeat of a no
never.detail: When someone declines a plan, treat it as settled. Revisit only if they raise it. Repetition of a question is pressure, whatever the tone.

power_moves.name: The unilateral decree
power_moves.how_it_works: One partner decides something large and presents it as already done, framing it as a shared good. The other may feel admiration and lose the chance to object before it lands.
power_moves.defense: Say what you would have wanted discussed before the decision. Ask whether future choices of that size will be brought to you first. If the answer is no, decide what you will do with that.

power_moves.name: The credit handoff
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone describes a joint project in the first person, and the other person's work quietly disappears from the account. Over time the story belongs to one narrator.
power_moves.defense: In the moment, add your part without heat. Say what you did and when. Later, ask for a shared version when telling the story to others.

power_moves.name: The announced outcome
power_moves.how_it_works: A promise is repeated in public settings, which makes it feel closer to done. Private arrangements may still be missing, and the gap is easy to overlook.
power_moves.defense: Ask for one date and one action. What happens next Tuesday. Who calls whom. Write it down together and check it once.

power_moves.name: The distant beneficiary
power_moves.how_it_works: Care is described for people far away while a partner's ordinary needs are not named. The generosity sounds large, and the partner may feel petty for raising anything.
power_moves.defense: Name one concrete need of your own this week. Ask directly whether your partner can meet it. Their answer tells you where you actually sit.

power_moves.name: The formal notice
power_moves.how_it_works: A serious change is delivered as a statement with no room for response. The formality discourages questions and makes hesitation seem like disloyalty.
power_moves.defense: Ask for time before you respond. Say you will answer tomorrow. Use the interval to decide what you consent to and what you decline.

leverage.point: You can ask for the terms before the announcement
leverage.detail: Next time a partner presents a plan as settled, ask what was agreed and by whom. If you were not part of the agreement, say you want to be before the next one. Test mutuality by seeing whether your answer changes anything.

leverage.point: You can name your own contribution
leverage.detail: On a shared project, agree at the start who did what and say it the same way to friends. Test it by asking your partner to repeat the account back. Differences show up early and can be fixed.

leverage.point: You can set the check-in date
leverage.detail: Instead of trusting a promise, propose a specific day to review how it is going. Put it in both calendars. Test mutuality by noticing whether they add their own marker or leave the follow-up entirely to you.

leverage.point: You can choose what you help with
leverage.detail: Offer the help you can actually give and decline the rest plainly. Gratitude you cannot back with action is not required. Test mutuality by seeing whether your no is accepted without a campaign to reverse it.

leverage.point: You can leave a settled no alone
leverage.detail: If a partner has declined something and you want it, say once that you are still interested, then stop. Test mutuality by watching whether they return to it on their own. Your agency includes accepting the answer.

closest.rationale: He announced from the National Palace the expropriation decree, publicly defining the decision on petroleum ownership and the means of enacting it through a formal declaration.

cousin.tell: Unlike a narrator staging a vivid scene of oilfields, Cárdenas stood in the National Palace and gave a decree that named who lost and who gained, making the petroleum transfer itself the spoken outcome.

basis.observation: The address framed the step as the nation reclaiming petroleum wealth long exploited by foreign firms, converting a legal instrument into a publicly declarable outcome.

sections.identity: As President of Uruguay, José Mujica told the 2012 Rio+20 summit that the crisis was political, not ecological, and urged a culture not governed by the market.

matches.why: At Rio+20, Mujica asked international delegates to consider whether a consumption model associated with rich societies could extend to everyone. That turned a conversation about producing more into one about what a good life requires.

pattern: Mujica's Rio+20 address moved the argument about consumption away from nature and onto people with choices. He asked whether the consumption model of wealthy societies could extend to billions, then named the crisis as political. The move is easy to picture: a table set for a few, and a question about who gets a place when everyone arrives. That reframing puts habits, not weather, at the center of a shared problem.

On 20 December 2013, Mujica signed the cannabis regulation law, his name first among the signing officials, establishing state control over cannabis. Whatever one thinks of the policy, the act shows a preference for rules written down over arrangements left informal. In ordinary terms, it resembles putting a shared household agreement on paper instead of letting assumptions pile up until someone feels cheated. The clarity arrives with costs attached, which is the point of writing it down.

Law No. 19075, promulgated on 3 May 2013 with Minister Ricardo Ehrlich, enacted equal marriage norms and sent the text to the National Registry of Laws and Decrees. The step was procedural and public, a signature and an order to publish. For a couple, the comparable move is deciding when a private understanding becomes something both people can point to. Publication matters because it lets each person see the same terms rather than remember them differently.

In a March 2014 M24 radio broadcast, Mujica called accepting Guantánamo detainees a matter of principle, inalienable and non-negotiable, and said he had asked Barack Obama to free three Cubans in exchange. A firm line and a request sat in the same breath. A reader might recognize the shape: holding one condition while naming what you hope for in return, so the other person is not left guessing.

text: Listen for whether a person names a problem as a choice people make or as weather that happens to them. The Rio+20 framing treated consumption as habits within human control. In conversation, that sounds like 'we keep spending on this' rather than 'money is just tight.' One phrasing leaves room for a partner to adjust and the other quietly assigns blame to circumstance.

Listen for the moment a person writes something down or insists it be clear. The cannabis and equal marriage steps both moved understandings into public, shared form. With a partner, the comparable signal is someone who says 'let's agree on this' rather than relying on memory. Listen too for whether they name what they want in return, as the exchange remark did, instead of leaving the ask buried.
examples: President José Mujica signed the 2013 cannabis regulation law, promulgated on 20 December, establishing state control over cannabis. His name appears first among the signing officials on the legislation.

At the June 2012 Rio+20 summit, Uruguay's President José Mujica questioned whether the consumption model of wealthy societies could extend to billions, saying the great challenge is that the crisis is political rather than ecological and urging another culture not governed by the market.

In his March 2014 M24 radio broadcast, President José Mujica called accepting Guantánamo detainees a matter of principle, inalienable and non-negotiable, and said he asked Barack Obama to free three Cubans in exchange.

José Mujica, as President of Uruguay, promulgated Law No. 19075 on 3 May 2013, enacting equal marriage norms, and signed the promulgation together with Minister Ricardo Ehrlich, ordering publication in the National Registry of Laws and Decrees.

spectrum.interested: At the electronics store on a rainy Saturday, one person stands in front of a 65-inch screen showing a slow pan over a mountain lake. "That's not bad," they say, then add, after a pause, "I'm not saying we need it." They leave the sticker price turned toward the other person and step back half a pace, so the next sentence is a real choice rather than a nudge.
spectrum.invested: By Tuesday a tape measure lies on the living-room floor, its metal tongue extended along the wall under the window. They compare where the old stand would sit and whether the lamp stays. One sketches the speaker placements on a receipt; the other checks the return window and writes it down. Shopping becomes a shared afternoon with sandwiches, not a surprise delivery.
spectrum.done: On Saturday one of them says, flatly, "I don't want the bigger screen in this room." The other answers, "Okay," and puts the tape measure in a drawer. A reader hearing that can ask once whether there's a version worth revisiting, then act separately: hang the curtains, book a matinee, or let the subject rest without renegotiating it weekly.

works.point: Ask what a rule is for
works.detail: When a partner proposes an agreement, ask what problem it solves. Write one sentence together. If neither of you can state the purpose, the rule may be decoration. A clear purpose makes the rule easier to keep and easier to revise later.

State what you are asking for alongside what you offer. For example, 'I will handle the bills this month if you take the calls to the landlord.' Spoken exchanges remove guessing. If the other person counters, that is negotiation, not rejection.

Set a weekly moment to look at shared costs together. Keep it short and on the calendar. The point is not surveillance but a shared picture. Couples who can both see the same numbers argue less about who remembered what.

Decide which of your conditions are firm and which are negotiable, then say so plainly. 'This one is not moving, that one I can flex.' People respond better to a clear map than to a blur of resistance that looks like stubbornness.

If a partner declines an agreement, accept it and pause. Ask what they would prefer instead. Do not keep rephrasing the same request until fatigue does the work. A no answered with patience tells you more than a yes given under pressure.

never.point: Do not reframe to win
never.detail: Turning every disagreement into a political question can make a partner feel like an audience. If you reframe, say why in plain words and check whether they agree with the frame. Otherwise the conversation becomes a contest you have quietly decided to referee.

never.point: Do not sign in haste
never.detail: A dramatic gesture can feel like commitment. At home, a sudden agreement made in a charged moment often needs a second look. Wait a day and reread it together. If either of you flinches, revise before acting.

never.point: Do not trade a principle for peace
never.detail: A firm condition is not a bargaining chip to spend whenever the mood sours. If you surrender it to end an argument, resentment usually follows. Say clearly which things will not move and let the other person decide how to respond.

never.point: Do not publish without consent
never.detail: Sharing a couple's private arrangement with friends or family can feel like accountability to one person and betrayal to the other. Ask first, every time. The answer may change by topic, and that is normal.

never.point: Do not treat a request as loyalty test
never.detail: When you ask for something, make the refusal survivable. 'I can hear a no on this' keeps the conversation honest. A request that punishes refusal is not a request any more, and the other person will start editing what they tell you.

power_moves.name: The reframe
power_moves.how_it_works: You shift the topic from circumstances to choices so the other person sees their own part. It can open a stuck conversation, and it can also make someone feel cornered if the shift arrives without warning.
power_moves.defense: Say, 'I notice we changed the subject. Can we finish the first question?' Naming the move keeps you in the conversation rather than following wherever it goes.

power_moves.name: The written term
power_moves.how_it_works: You put an understanding on paper or repeat it aloud so both people hold the same version. It reduces misremembering and can feel cold to someone who prefers spoken warmth.
power_moves.defense: Ask, 'Can we read it together and change what is wrong?' A draft is not a verdict. Agreeing to edit before signing keeps the document useful.

power_moves.name: The firm line with a request
power_moves.how_it_works: You state one firm condition and name what you hope for in return, the way the exchange remark did. It is honest, and it can pressure a partner who has not had time to think.
power_moves.defense: Answer the request separately from the condition. 'I hear the line. Give me a day on the ask.' Separate clocks prevent one from becoming hostage to the other.

power_moves.name: The public commitment
power_moves.how_it_works: You make a decision visible, which raises the stakes and invites others to hold you to it. It can be sincere, and it can leave a partner exposed if they were not consulted.
power_moves.defense: Ask, 'Who will know, and did we both agree to that?' Visibility is a choice the two of you make together, not one person announcing on behalf of two.

power_moves.name: The moral framing
power_moves.how_it_works: You describe a preference as a matter of principle, which signals seriousness and can shut down negotiation. Sometimes it is true. Sometimes it ends a conversation that still had room.
power_moves.defense: Ask, 'Which part is principle and which part is preference?' A clear answer tells you where you stand and what can still be discussed without disrespect.

leverage.detail: You choose how quickly a shared agreement is made. Ask for a day, a week, or a reread. A partner who respects your pace will wait. If waiting becomes a grievance, you have learned something useful about how decisions will feel later.

Write your own short list of what you want from a shared routine, then compare it with theirs. Look for overlap and for one item where you can trade. Mutuality shows when both lists change after the conversation rather than one list disappearing.

Keep two questions ready. 'What problem does this solve for you?' and 'What would you like back?' Ask them at a calm moment. Repeated answers that match actions are a test of mutuality you can run without drama.

Practice declining a request out loud in a low-stakes setting, such as a weekend plan. Notice how the other person responds to a simple no. Their reaction to small refusals tells you how a larger one will land.

Keep enough separate resources, time and friendships that leaving a bad agreement remains possible. This is not a threat. It is a quiet condition that lets you negotiate honestly instead of accepting terms out of fear. You decide when to use it.

closest.rationale: At Rio+20, Mujica asked international delegates to consider whether a consumption model associated with rich societies could extend to everyone. That turned a conversation about producing more into one about what a good life requires.

cousin.tell: A storyteller could follow one household through a day of buying and discarding. At Rio+20 Mujica challenged delegates to examine the assumption that copying the wealthiest societies was an adequate goal.

basis.style: Questioning the goal behind greater consumption
basis.observation: Mujica raised the scale of consumption itself as a matter for debate. He treated patterns of everyday demand as part of the environmental question, alongside the technologies and policies governments were discussing.

sections.identity: Chilean President Salvador Allende denounced external and ITT pressure on Chile in a December 1972 United Nations General Assembly address.

matches.why: In his December 1972 UN General Assembly speech Allende recast external pressure on Chile as a sovereign matter, detailed ITT's plan to overthrow his government, and named the grievance before an intergovernmental body rather than privately.

pattern: When Allende sent Congress a bill in December 1970 to add the word nacionalizar to Article 10 of the 1925 Constitution, he was attempting to change a defining rule rather than win a momentary argument. The promulgating decree came in July 1971. A person who wants a relationship to run differently often starts by naming the rule itself, such as what counts as shared money or shared time.

Not every grievance belongs in private. In December 1972 the Assembly heard about an October 1971 ITT document laying out an 18-point plan to bring the government down within six months. He took the complaint to an intergovernmental body instead of keeping it behind one closed door. A partner might similarly ask a trusted friend to sit in on a recurring money conversation.

Allende endorsed Unidad Popular's December 1969 program, which pledged half a liter of milk daily for every Chilean child. It was a plain, measurable commitment attached to a coalition, not a vague promise of better days. A couple planning a move can copy that habit. Write down the amount, the day, the person responsible, and check it after a month.

The last words came through Radio Magallanes on 11 September 1973, in a broadcast that also carried a declaration from the Communist Party's Political Commission. The message went out through a shared channel rather than a private one. In a household, choosing which channel carries hard news matters. A weekly ten-minute talk at the kitchen table can keep important things from arriving only in a crisis.

text: Listen for whether the other person can state the specific ask rather than the general complaint. Instead of saying things have been unfair, they might say, I want us to split the grocery bill evenly starting this month. A precise request is easier to answer and easier to decline honestly without either person guessing at hidden meanings.

Listen for where they choose to raise a hard subject. Someone who brings a recurring problem to the dinner table when both are calm is treating it as shared business. Someone who saves it for a late-night argument is treating it as ammunition. You can say, I would rather talk about this Saturday morning than at midnight.
examples: In December 1970, President Salvador Allende sent Congress a bill to amend the 1925 Constitution's Article 10, adding the word "nacionalizar" to the right of property; Allende signed the promulgating decree on 15 July 1971.

On 4 December 1972, Salvador Allende addressed the United Nations General Assembly, denouncing external pressures against Chile and describing the ITT's plan to overthrow his government within six months.
On 11 September 1973, Salvador Allende delivered his last words through Radio Magallanes in a special broadcast that also included a declaration by the Communist Party's Political Commission.

As Unidad Popular's presidential candidate, Allende endorsed the coalition's basic program of December 1969, which pledged to guarantee half a liter of milk daily as a ration for all Chilean children.

spectrum.interested: At the Thursday market, one person lifts a jar of chili crisp, turns it toward the other, and says, “This could go on the noodles—unless you’d rather keep dinner plain.” They name two open evenings and add, “Pick whichever suits, or say none.” Nothing obliges an answer that day; the evening is offered, not assumed.
spectrum.invested: By Saturday, a grocery list sits on the counter in two handwritings: sesame oil, scallions, a specific brand of frozen dumplings. One person texts a photo of the receipt, the other answers with “I’ll bring the good vinegar.” The plan has a time, a door code, and a shared task, each person having moved one concrete thing forward.
spectrum.done: When the invitation resurfaces, one replies plainly, “I’d rather keep dinners to the group for now.” A reader can take that sentence at face value, send a short “Thanks for telling me,” and then decide their own next step—whether to propose a group meal, wait, or step back—without treating a slow reply as a verdict.

works.point: Name the rule, not the mood
works.detail: Say which arrangement you want to change and when it should start. We agreed to alternate cooking, and I would like to switch to whoever is home first. A clear rule is easier to accept, revise, or refuse than a complaint about feeling unappreciated.

works.point: Bring it to the right table
works.detail: Choose the setting where the subject can actually be resolved. A money worry belongs in a calm conversation with the person who shares the account. A family tension may need the sibling who is involved. Taking it to the wrong listener leaves the real conversation untouched.

Pick a commitment small enough to check. Half an hour of phones-down time on Wednesdays. One shared meal on Sundays. Put it where both of you can see it, and look at it after two weeks. A promise with a number is easier to keep or to renegotiate.

works.point: Use a shared channel for hard news
works.detail: Agree in advance how difficult topics travel. A weekly ten-minute check-in, a shared note, a walk after dinner. When something heavy arrives, you already know where to put it. This keeps bad news from landing only during an argument or a crisis.

works.point: Ask for a specific thing you can deliver
works.detail: Make requests concrete. I would like you to text me when you are running late. I would like to choose the weekend plan together. Specific requests can be met, measured and thanked. They also make it easy for the other person to say what they need in return.

never.point: Do not bargain with a threat
never.detail: Saying you will leave unless a rule changes turns a conversation into a contest. State what you want and what you will do if it does not happen. Keep the second part about your own choices, such as stepping back from a shared plan, and say it once.

never.point: Do not announce a rule you have not discussed
never.detail: A decision made alone and presented as settled invites resentment. Bring the proposal early. We could try this for a month, what do you think. If the other person says no, you have learned something useful without a fight.

never.point: Do not keep score out loud
never.detail: Counting favors turns care into a ledger. I did the dishes four times this week is a bill, not a request. If the balance bothers you, ask for one change directly and leave the history out of it.

never.point: Do not use a friend as a messenger
never.detail: Asking someone else to raise your concern with your partner adds a third person to a two-person problem. Say the difficult sentence yourself, even badly. If you need support, ask a friend for a listening ear beforehand, not for delivery.

never.point: Do not treat a public promise as private proof
never.detail: A pledge made in front of others can still be real, but it is not evidence of how someone behaves at home. Watch what happens on an ordinary Tuesday. Judge the small, unglamorous actions rather than the announcement.

power_moves.name: The Reframer
power_moves.how_it_works: When a conversation stalls, the person asks the same question from a different angle. Instead of why are you always late, they ask what makes leaving on time hard. This can open a new answer, and it can also feel like being steered.
power_moves.defense: You can say, I noticed we changed the subject, and I still want to answer the first question. If the new angle is fair, answer it and return to your point. If it keeps sliding away from what you raised, name that and ask to stay with one topic.

power_moves.name: The Documented Complaint
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone arrives with dates, figures and a list of past incidents to show the problem is real. This can be useful when a pattern is being denied. It can also overwhelm the other person, who then defends the details instead of the issue.
power_moves.defense: Ask for one example you can work on. Say, I hear the pattern matters, and I can only fix one thing at a time. Let us choose the next two weeks and check then. This keeps the conversation from becoming a trial of the past.

power_moves.name: The Public Appeal
power_moves.how_it_works: A private grievance is raised in front of friends or family, with the hope that witnesses will make the other person take it seriously. The pressure can produce a quick agreement. It can also humiliate the person and harden their position.
power_moves.defense: Say quietly, I would rather finish this just the two of us, and set a time later that day. Afterward, be clear that future disagreements should be raised privately first. If someone keeps bringing outside witnesses into personal matters, treat that as important information about how they handle conflict.

power_moves.name: The Coalition Pledge
power_moves.how_it_works: A shared promise is made concrete and small, with a number and a date attached. Everyone involved knows exactly what was agreed. This builds trust when it is kept. It can become a trap when one person sets the number without asking whether it is workable.
power_moves.defense: Before you agree, ask who does which part and what happens if life gets in the way. Say, I can commit to Sundays, not every evening. A pledge you helped shape is one you can keep without resentment.

power_moves.name: The Early Alert
power_moves.how_it_works: A problem is named before it grows, while it is still small and fixable. This can prevent later damage. It can also sound like constant vigilance, where every minor thing becomes a formal warning and the other person feels monitored.
power_moves.defense: Say, thank you for telling me early, and ask how big it feels. Then decide together whether it needs a fix now or only a note. If small alerts arrive daily, ask whether some could wait for the weekly check-in.

leverage.detail: You choose when recurring conversations happen. A ten-minute talk on Sunday evening is yours to propose. Test for mutuality by seeing whether the other person shows up for it twice without a reminder. If they do, the arrangement is real for both of you.

You decide which accounts, plans and worries are joint and which stay yours. Say the line plainly. My savings stay mine, and the grocery costs are shared. Test whether the other person respects the boundary after you name it, not only in the first week.

You can request one concrete change and give it a time frame. We alternate the school run for the next month. Test whether the change actually happens and whether the other person offers one of their own without being asked.

You can refuse to settle a private disagreement in front of others. Say, I will talk about this with you at home. Test whether that request is honored the next time a dispute begins with an audience nearby.

You can end a conversation that has turned into a contest of documents or a public trial. Say, I am pausing this, and we will pick it up Thursday at seven. Test whether the other person returns to the agreed time. If they do not, you have learned what follow-through means here and can decide what you will offer next.

closest.rationale: In his December 1972 UN General Assembly speech Allende recast external pressure on Chile as a sovereign matter, detailed ITT's plan to overthrow his government, and named the grievance before an intergovernmental body rather than privately.

cousin.tell: Unlike the Dissenter, who tells allies face-to-face where he disagrees, Allende took an external grievance to the UN General Assembly and described ITT's plan before an intergovernmental body.

basis.observation: The same address pressed the Assembly on external interference while citing a specific ITT document dated October 1971 that outlined an 18-point plan to bring down his government within six months.

sections.identity: Chilean president Patricio Aylwin publicly presented the Rettig Commission report in 1991 and asked pardon for documented human rights victims.

matches.why: Aylwin presented the Rettig Commission’s findings on dictatorship-era human rights violations to Chileans on television. He took a report assembled by investigators and made its account of victims a matter of national acknowledgment.

pattern: The televised address in March 1991 put a nameable weight on the presidency. A report could have sat on a shelf, read by committees and filed away. Instead, the office that could act stood in front of the country and asked forgiveness for violations it had catalogued. The observable choice was to attach a public request to a public finding. In a partnership, that translates to saying the hard thing out loud to the person affected rather than leaving a note in a drawer for them to find.

Serving as spokesman for the coalition against Pinochet's continuation meant carrying a shared case in front of many audiences. A spokesman does not own the message alone. He tests whether the words hold when different groups are listening. The parallel for a couple is modest. When you speak for both of you to family or friends, the question is whether your partner would recognize the sentence as theirs too. Speaking for a shared position asks for rehearsal, not improvisation.

The negotiations over fifty-four proposed constitutional reforms after the No victory show a willingness to sit across from an opponent and work through a list, item by item. That is unglamorous labor. It suggests a tolerance for partial movement rather than a single dramatic win. A household version exists. Two people with a long list of disagreements can either demand the whole list resolved tonight or take the items one at a time. The second is slower and often survives longer.

The August 1991 press conference in Buenos Aires described border and economic agreements with Argentina that settled twenty-two of twenty-four border points and sent Laguna del Desierto to international arbitration. The pattern worth noting is the handling of the remainder. Two points could not be closed, and they were named and routed elsewhere. A couple can borrow the shape without the diplomacy. After a long argument, name what is settled, name what is not, and decide who or what will hold the open item so it does not quietly poison the rest.

text: Listen for whether a person names what they actually want changed. A request with a target is different from a mood broadcast. When your partner says the evenings feel thin, you can ask what one evening next week would look like if it were better. The reply tells you whether they have thought about a concrete change or are only ventilating. Neither is wrong. You just need to know which conversation you are in.

Listen for the moment someone speaks about a third party. How they describe a friend's mistake or a colleague's failure shows how they might describe yours. If every story casts the absent person as foolish, expect the same framing when you are absent. If they can hold two sides without flattening them, that is worth noticing. You are not judging character. You are gathering information about how conflict gets narrated in their life.
examples: On 4 March 1991, President Patricio Aylwin addressed the nation on television to present the Rettig Commission report, and in the name of the state he asked forgiveness of the victims of the human rights violations documented in it.

In 1988 Patricio Aylwin served as spokesman for the Concertación de Partidos por el No, the coalition campaigning against Pinochet's continuation in the October 5 plebiscite. After the No victory, he took part in negotiations with President Augusto Pinochet over fifty-four proposed constitutional reforms.

On 2 August 1991, at a press conference in Buenos Aires, Chilean President Patricio Aylwin highlighted the border and economic integration agreements signed with Argentina, which resolved 22 of 24 border points and submitted the Laguna del Desierto case to international arbitration.

On 5 October 1993, Congress passed the Indigenous Law (Law 19,253), which recognized indigenous peoples and created CONADI. At its promulgation ceremony in Nueva Imperial, President Patricio Aylwin called the law a transcendental step, even though the constitutional reform recognizing indigenous peoples remained pending.

spectrum.interested: Mira texts Jo after the fence post goes down: “Saw the ambulance. I can drop off soup or just leave a bag on the porch—entirely up to you.” Jo answers with a thumbs-up and nothing else for two days. Mira sends one more message—a photo of the dented post—and notes she’ll hold off until Jo says otherwise.
spectrum.invested: Thursday, Jo leaves a grocery bag with two cans of tomato soup and a note reading “porch light works.” Mira tapes a flashlight outside and moves a spare key to the mailbox, texting the code. They split the cost of a new post by leaving cash in an envelope. Both repeatedly confirm the other still wants help.
spectrum.done: Saturday, Jo says, “Please stop leaving things—I need quiet this week.” Mira replies, “Understood; I won’t knock,” then decides whether to check back in ten days. Observable acts: no deliveries, no doorbell. Jo may later leave a note on the mailbox; Mira can accept that as one signal among several and act according to her own limits.

works.detail: Name one concrete change you want rather than a general complaint. Say you would like Sunday evenings without phones. A target gives the other person something to answer. Vague dissatisfaction invites vague reassurance.

Before speaking for both of you to family, check the sentence with your partner. Read it aloud and ask if they would sign it. Adjust until both of you can. This prevents one person becoming the accidental spokesperson for a position the other never agreed to.

When several disagreements are tangled, pick one. Say you want to settle the money question this month and leave the holiday question for later. Partial movement is still movement. A finished item builds trust for the next.

At the end of a long talk, say what is settled and what is not. Ask who will hold the open item and when you will return to it. Written notes help. An open item with a date is different from an open item left to drift.

If you said something sharp, name it and say what you meant instead. Do not wait for the other person to raise it. A short specific repair lands better than a long apology that asks them to comfort you for having said it.

never.point: Do not let a report sit
never.detail: If you have learned something that affects your partner, tell them. Holding information because the timing feels awkward turns a small honesty problem into a large one. Choose a calm moment and say it plainly. Then let them respond without managing their reaction.

never.point: Do not speak for them unasked
never.detail: Avoid telling friends what your partner thinks about a shared matter. Even a small assumption can put words in their mouth. If a question comes up, say you would rather they answer. This protects both of you from cleanup later.

never.point: Do not demand the whole list
never.detail: Insisting every disagreement resolve in one sitting produces exhaustion and false agreement. Some items need time and outside help. Say which ones you can handle now and which need a later conversation. Pretending all is settled is worse than naming the gap.

never.point: Do not confuse apology with absolution
never.detail: A public or private request for forgiveness is a beginning, not a receipt. If you apologize, expect the other person to take time. Do not ask them to confirm you are forgiven. Their pace is theirs. Your job is to change the behavior the apology named.

never.point: Do not narrate third parties as fools
never.detail: When you tell stories about other people, watch how you cast them. If every anecdote makes someone stupid, your partner will notice. They may wonder how you describe them. Try telling one story where the other person had a reasonable case.

power_moves.name: The public ask
power_moves.how_it_works: You say the difficult thing where it can be heard by the person it concerns, rather than hinting through friends or waiting for them to guess. It may relieve pressure and clarify what you want. If your partner seems startled, give them time and offer one concrete next step rather than pressing for an immediate response.
power_moves.defense: If someone makes a public ask about you without warning, you can say you need a day before answering. Ask for the request in writing or repeat it back. Reply when you are ready. You are allowed to decline the framing as well as the request.

power_moves.name: The coalition voice
power_moves.how_it_works: You speak for a shared position to outsiders and check the wording with your partner first. Done well, it prevents confusion and keeps you both aligned. If your partner hesitates over a phrase, revise it together before anyone else hears it.
power_moves.defense: If you learn your partner described your shared view in words you would not use, say so privately and ask what they meant. Offer your own wording. Avoid correcting them in front of the others unless safety requires it.

power_moves.name: The item-by-item table
power_moves.how_it_works: You bring a list of disagreements and work through one at a time, agreeing on what is closed and what remains. It can lower the temperature by making progress visible. Ask your partner whether the pace suits them. Some people need rest between items.
power_moves.defense: If a long negotiation leaves you drained, say you want to stop and resume on a named day. Write down what was agreed so the pause does not reopen everything. You can also decline to keep negotiating past a stated limit.

power_moves.name: The named remainder
power_moves.how_it_works: You close what you can and openly route the rest to a later conversation, a counselor, or a written list. This keeps unresolved matters visible without forcing a false finish. Say who holds the item and when it returns. Your partner may prefer a different holder.
power_moves.defense: If someone declares a topic closed while you still have questions, say you are not finished. Ask for a specific date to return to it. You can also ask that a neutral third person join the next round.

power_moves.name: The formal acknowledgment
power_moves.how_it_works: You name a harm plainly and ask for pardon without demanding a particular response. The effect can be relief or renewed anger. Both are possible. Follow with a change in behavior. Ask what would help, and accept that the answer may take time.
power_moves.defense: If an apology arrives with pressure to forgive, you can say thank you and that you need time. You are not required to grant absolution on the spot. Ask what will be different next month. Watch the behavior rather than the words.

leverage.point: You can set the pace of disclosure
leverage.detail: Decide what you will share and when. You are allowed to say you want to hold a piece of information until you have thought it through. Test mutuality by noticing whether the other person respects the pause or pushes against it.

leverage.point: You can ask for a target
leverage.detail: Turn a complaint into a request with a shape. Ask for one behavior change and a time frame. Test mutuality by seeing whether they ask for something in return and whether both requests get taken seriously.

leverage.point: You can decline to speak for both
leverage.detail: If you are asked to represent a shared view you have not agreed on, say you would rather each of you answer. Test mutuality by watching whether your partner backs you up or undermines the boundary in front of others.

leverage.point: You can leave an item open on purpose
leverage.detail: Not every disagreement needs a verdict tonight. Name the item, set a return date, and stop. Test mutuality by checking whether the other person honors the return date without you having to chase it.

leverage.point: You can accept or refuse an apology
leverage.detail: A request for pardon is not a command. You may say thank you and take time, or say the apology does not match the harm. Test mutuality by observing whether the person can hear refusal without withdrawing affection or escalating.

closest.rationale: Aylwin presented the Rettig Commission’s findings on dictatorship-era human rights violations to Chileans on television. He took a report assembled by investigators and made its account of victims a matter of national acknowledgment.

cousin.tell: An advocate could take families’ demands to officials and ask for an investigation. When Aylwin addressed Chile in 1991, the commission had reported: his particular responsibility was making its findings public.

basis.style: Bringing the Rettig findings before the country
basis.observation: The commission did the investigative work. The president’s part was to face the public with its findings and ask forgiveness in the name of the state, placing responsibility beyond the families who had pressed to be heard.

sections.identity: Argentina's president Raúl Alfonsín decreed in December 1983 that the military juntas be tried for human rights crimes.

matches.why: Signed Decreto 158 on 13 December 1983, sending the military juntas' human rights crimes to trial and fixing a judicial route before any outcome existed.

pattern: Three days into the presidency, Alfonsín signed Decreto 158, which sent the juntas' human rights crimes to trial and fixed a judicial route before any outcome existed. The proceduralist move is to agree how a disputed decision will be made and make the outcome checkable. In a shared household, that could look like writing down how you will choose a new flat: who lists options, who visits, what budget rules apply, and when you will review the list together.

On 15 December 1983, Decreto 187 created the Comisión Nacional sobre la Desaparición de Personas to investigate disappearances and locate abducted children. The commission's job was to gather information, not to deliver a verdict in advance. A parallel in ordinary life is agreeing to keep a shared log of what happens when plans change, so both people can look at the same record later instead of relying on memory or goodwill.

In July 1984, Alfonsín called a non-binding popular consultation on the peace treaty with Chile, inviting citizens to express an opinion without making the result obligatory. The consultation had a defined question and a defined use. Couples can borrow the shape without the statecraft: a trial run of living together for a set period, with a clear question (does this rhythm suit us?) and a clear date to decide what happens next.

On 24 April 1987, Alfonsín signed the Acta de Compromiso Histórico in defense of democracy and gave a national address declaring the Semana Santa crisis closed. The written commitment named what was being defended and marked an end point. A useful everyday version is a short written agreement after a hard patch: what each person will do differently, how you will know it is working, and when you will check in again.

text: Listen for whether a partner states the method before the outcome. Someone who says, 'Here is how I think we should decide this, and here is how you can check it,' is offering a process you can inspect. Someone who only announces the verdict leaves you guessing at the rules. The difference matters more in small decisions than in grand ones.

Pay attention to how a person handles a non-binding question. Do they treat your opinion as information they asked for, or as a vote they can overrule? A partner who asks, 'What do you think we should do about the weekend?' and then waits is showing you the difference between consultation and decoration. Notice whether they return to your answer later.
examples: Raúl Alfonsín signed Decreto 187 on 15 December 1983, creating the Comisión Nacional sobre la Desaparición de Personas to investigate disappearances and locate abducted children, shortly after taking office.
Raúl Alfonsín, as president, signed Decree 158 on 13 December 1983, ordering the trial of the military juntas that governed Argentina from 1976 to 1983 for grave human rights violations.

On 26 July 1984, President Raúl Alfonsín called a non-binding, non-obligatory popular consultation so citizens could express their opinion on accepting the Tratado de Paz y Amistad with Chile, signed later in the Vatican.

On 24 April 1987, Raúl Alfonsín signed the Acta de Compromiso Histórico in defense of democracy at the Casa Rosada and gave a national radio and television address declaring the Semana Santa crisis closed and reaffirming the defense of democracy.

spectrum.interested: A spare key on a nail, a folded map of bus routes, and one text: “My cousin needs the guest room Saturday—only if it works for you.” The offer stays open; the sender adds, “Say no and I’ll tell her tonight.” Notice the explicit permission to decline and the concrete deadline offered, then watch whether a reply names a time to decide rather than a vague maybe.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday, two calendars sit open on the kitchen table, a spare blanket airs over a chair, and someone writes “hold guest room” on a sticky note. A reply arrives: “I can move my call to ten, so she has the room until noon.” These are checkable acts—a held slot, a moved appointment, a note on the fridge—showing both people putting something real on the line.
spectrum.done: Saturday morning, one says plainly, “I can’t host after Tuesday—I need that room for work.” The other answers, “Understood; I’ll tell her to book elsewhere,” and writes it down. A reader can respect that by not re-asking, by naming their own alternative date in writing, and by leaving the closed boundary closed while deciding whether to offer a different week.

works.detail: Before a tense talk, agree on the one question you are answering. Write it on a sticky note. If the conversation drifts, point to the note. This keeps a disagreement from becoming a referendum on the whole relationship.

Keep a note both people can see about who is doing what by when. Review it together on a set day. A shared list turns 'you promised' into 'here is what we wrote,' which is easier to discuss without scoring points.

For a big step, propose a trial with a clear end date and a question to answer afterward. For example, live together for two months and then ask, 'Does this rhythm work for both of us?' The trial is real and so is the exit.

After a hard patch, write a short agreement: what each person will do, how you will know it is working, and when you will check in. Keep it to one page. The point is a shared reference, not a legal document.

When a decision feels stuck, say where and how you will make it. 'Let's decide at the kitchen table on Sunday with the budget open' is a forum. A forum reduces the chance that the louder person wins by default.

never.point: Do not announce a verdict as a conversation
never.detail: If you have already decided, say so plainly rather than staging a discussion. A fake consultation breeds resentment. 'I have made up my mind about this, and I want to tell you why' is honest and leaves room for a response.

never.point: Do not keep the method secret
never.detail: A process only you understand is not a shared process. If you have a rule for how chores get divided, write it down or say it aloud. Hidden rules make the other person feel tested rather than included.

never.point: Do not use a trial as a threat
never.detail: A trial run works when both people can say no without punishment. If the trial is framed as a last chance you will use against them later, it becomes pressure. Say what happens if either person wants to stop, and mean it.

never.point: Do not let a written agreement replace listening
never.detail: A page of commitments is a tool, not a shield. If your partner says the agreement is not working, the next move is to talk, not to cite the text. The writing serves the relationship, not the other way around.

never.point: Do not borrow authority you do not have
never.detail: Public titles, family status or being the one who 'usually decides' are not a mandate. In a two-person decision, ask for agreement in plain words. If you catch yourself saying 'this is how we do it,' check whether the other person ever said yes.

power_moves.name: The published method
power_moves.how_it_works: One person states the steps for making a decision before the decision is made, so the other can see the path and object to it early. This can build trust because the process is visible and repeatable. If a partner does this, you can say, 'I like that you told me the steps. Can we add a review after the first month?' If you do it, write the steps where both can see them.
power_moves.defense: When someone presents a method, your respectful response is to test it with a small question. 'What happens if we disagree at step three?' shows you are engaged. You are not obliged to accept a method just because it is clear. Clarity is an invitation to negotiate, not a command to comply.

power_moves.name: The commission shape
power_moves.how_it_works: A person proposes a fact-finding step before any blame is assigned, such as keeping a log of who does which chores for two weeks. This can lower defensiveness because the goal is information, not a verdict. If a partner suggests this, you can say, 'I will keep the log if you will, and we look at it together on Sunday.'
power_moves.defense: A fact-finding step should have a stated purpose and an end point. If a partner proposes a log but will not say what it is for, ask. You can agree to gather information without agreeing to be audited indefinitely. 'I will do this for two weeks, then we decide what it told us' keeps it mutual.

power_moves.name: The non-binding question
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone asks for your opinion without making your answer binding, which can make room for honesty. In everyday life this might sound like, 'I am leaning toward moving, but I want to hear how you feel before I treat it as settled.' If a partner does this, you can answer freely and then ask what they will do with your answer.
power_moves.defense: You can decline a consultation that feels like a performance. 'I would rather wait until you are ready to decide together' is a respectful limit, and so is asking, 'Will my answer change anything?' A non-binding question only helps if the asker is genuinely open to being moved.

power_moves.name: The written commitment
power_moves.how_it_works: After a conflict, one person proposes a short written agreement naming what each will do and when they will check in. This can turn vague promises into something both can point to. If a partner offers this, you can say, 'I will sign if we include what happens when one of us slips.'
power_moves.defense: A written commitment should be short and revisable. If a partner drafts a long document without your input, ask to write it together. You can say, 'I want one page and a date to review it.' You are allowed to decline a document that feels like a contract imposed on you.

power_moves.name: The closing statement
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone publicly or privately declares a difficult period closed and names what is being defended, such as calm evenings or honest money talk. This can provide relief and a shared marker. If a partner does this, you can say, 'I am glad you said that. What will we do differently this week?'
power_moves.defense: A closing statement is not a substitute for change. You can accept the gesture and still ask for specifics. 'I hear that you want this closed. I need to see the new routine for a month before I feel the same' is fair. No one else gets to declare closure on your behalf.

leverage.point: Ask for the method before the answer
leverage.detail: When a decision is coming, you can say, 'Before you tell me what you think we should do, can we agree how we will decide?' This tests whether the other person is willing to build a shared process. If they refuse, that is information you can use to decide your next step.

leverage.point: Propose a trial with an exit
leverage.detail: For a step that feels risky, suggest a time-limited test with a clear question at the end. 'Let's try this for six weeks and then ask whether it suited both of us.' You keep agency because the exit is named. A partner who will not accept an exit is showing you something about how they handle your limits.

leverage.point: Keep your own copy of the plan
leverage.detail: If you agree to a shared plan, write it down and keep your own copy. This is not suspicion; it is a check for mutuality. When the plan is reviewed, you can compare notes. If the other person objects to any written record, ask why.

leverage.point: Say no to a fake consultation
leverage.detail: If you are asked for an opinion but the decision is already made, you can say, 'I would rather you tell me it is decided than ask me as if it is open.' This protects your time and signals that you expect honest process. You can still discuss the decision without pretending it was joint.

You do not have to wait for a partner to schedule a check-in. Pick a date, put it in your calendar, and say, 'On the first of the month, can we look at how this is going?' A self-started review is a simple test of whether the other person shows up for the maintenance, not just the beginning.

closest.rationale: Signed Decreto 158 on 13 December 1983, sending the military juntas' human rights crimes to trial and fixing a judicial route before any outcome existed.

cousin.tell: Where an Open Book would simply pledge accountability aloud, Alfonsín filed decrees specifying the defendants and the violations, letting the paperwork carry the pledge.

basis.observation: Three days into the presidency he set the forum, the accused, and the charge by written decree, so the junta trial rested on a published method citizens could follow rather than a personal promise.

sections.identity: As President of Brazil, Lula da Silva traveled with Turkey's prime minister in 2010 to Tehran to seek a negotiated solution to Iran's nuclear dispute.

matches.why: In May 2010 Lula flew to Tehran with Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan to seek a negotiated solution with President Ahmadinejad, framing the trip as a joint search for a negotiated settlement.

pattern: Personal presence carried weight in the Tehran effort. Rather than sending a deputy with talking points, he boarded the plane with Recep Tayyip Erdogan and sat across from Ahmadinejad himself. The gesture said the matter was consequential enough to spend his own hours on it. In everyday terms, that looks like the difference between a partner who forwards an article about saving for a trip and one who opens a calendar and asks which week you both can take off.

The Tehran initiative was built as a joint search, not a solo performance. Two leaders from different countries presented a shared front, and the framing centered on finding terms rather than announcing a verdict. When two people try to settle a recurring argument about money or family visits, the same principle applies. Arriving together, with one agreed proposal, reads differently than arriving with a verdict already drafted and a second signature requested.

The Fome Zero rollout in January 2003 paired a public commitment with a structure. A decree installed the food security council to shape national policy, and the program was described in his speech as combat against hunger and social exclusion. Read modestly, the design lesson is that a promise gains weight when a specific group of people is named to carry it forward. Saying we should be more considerate is not the same as agreeing who does what by Friday.

The stadium gathering in São Bernardo do Campo took place during the March 1979 metalworkers’ strike. Earlier assemblies had already voted for the stoppage. Calling people together again gave workers a place to hear from one another while events unfolded. A decision at home can deserve a second conversation too, especially when the people affected by it learn something the original plan did not anticipate.

text: Listen for whether the other person treats a problem as shared or as yours to solve alone. The Tehran trip was framed as a joint search, which means someone had to say the word together out loud. In conversation, that sounds like a partner asking what would actually work for both of you, then waiting for an answer instead of filling the silence with a proposal you have not had time to weigh.

Listen for the difference between a named commitment and a warm sentiment. The food security council was set up so that responsibility had a home, not merely a speech. When a partner says they want things to improve, hear whether a specific action and a time follow. You are allowed to ask who does what and when, and to notice if the answer keeps sliding toward someday, we should really sort that out.
examples: On 30 January 2003, in Brasília, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva launched the Fome Zero program, describing it in a speech as a fight against hunger and social exclusion, and established by decree the Food Security Council (Consea), responsible for formulating the National Food Security Policy.

On October 20, 2003, Lula issued Provisional Measure 132, creating Bolsa Família. The measure brought existing federal cash-transfer initiatives into a unified program. A separate presidential decree established the working group that would coordinate the data systems.

During the March 1979 strike, Lula, then president of the São Bernardo do Campo and Diadema metalworkers’ union, called workers together at the Vila Euclides stadium. Earlier assemblies had already voted to strike on March 13.

In May 2010, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Turkish Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan traveled to Tehran to seek, with President Ahmadinejad, a negotiated solution to a dispute that threatened regional stability, as Lula himself recounted.
