spectrum.interested: At the bakery counter, Dana slides a printed schedule across the glass: Saturday's festival shift, marked with a red circle. "I could take your morning if you'd want the evening off—no pressure either way." Sam studies the sheet, taps the circled block, and says, "Maybe. Let me check one thing first." Nothing is promised; the printed page stays between them while the line moves.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday the schedule is on the fridge, held by a magnet shaped like a lemon. Sam texts a photo of a swapped name in pen, then brings two coffees to the Saturday briefing and asks which tasks Dana would rather not handle. They write initials beside the truck unloading and the ticket table, then agree to confirm Friday at six.
spectrum.done: Friday at six, Sam says plainly, "I can't do the full evening after all—two hours, then I'm gone." Dana nods, marks the limit on the sheet, and decides whether two hours is enough or whether to ask someone else. Respecting it means not renegotiating in the moment: thank them, adjust the plan, and leave the rest unspoken.

works.detail: After a conversation about chores, money or visits, send a short message restating what each of you agreed to. Ask the other person to correct anything wrong. A written summary is not distrust. It is the same instinct that turns a general pledge into a named responsibility, and it gives you both something concrete to revisit next week.

Some conflicts shrink when you stop discussing them across a kitchen table and go do something side by side. A walk, a drive, a shared errand can loosen a stuck exchange. Choose the setting deliberately and say why. If the issue is recurring, agree in advance that this particular outing is for listening and that decisions wait until you are both home.

Before a hard conversation, draft one option you believe the other person could genuinely accept. Present it as a starting point and ask what they would change. This mirrors the joint-search approach and prevents the familiar pattern where one person arrives with a finished plan and the other is expected to sign. One workable shared option beats three perfect ones only you want.

When you promise change, attach a person and a date. We should eat better becomes I will cook on Tuesdays and you shop on Sundays, starting this week. Vague goodwill fades quickly. Naming the carrier also lets the other person say no before the commitment hardens, which is fairer than discovering the gap later.

Set a specific moment to review how an agreement is going, perhaps two weeks out. Treat the check-in as routine rather than as an accusation. Ask what is working and what needs adjusting. Agreements that never get reviewed tend to drift back to old habits, and a scheduled look back makes revision ordinary instead of dramatic.

never.point: Do not announce a conclusion
never.detail: Arriving with a decision already locked and asking for a signature invites resentment. If you have made up your mind, say so honestly and let the other person respond. Presenting a fixed outcome as a negotiation wastes their time and teaches them that their input arrives too late to matter.

never.point: Do not use presence as proof
never.detail: Showing up to a difficult conversation is a start, not a settlement. Do not treat your willingness to sit down as evidence that the other person owes agreement. Presence earns a hearing. It does not purchase consent, and treating it that way turns a good-faith gesture into a debt you collect.

never.point: Do not schedule an ambush
never.detail: Springing a serious subject in front of friends or family corners the other person publicly. They will react to the audience rather than to you. Name the topic in advance, pick a private moment, and accept that they may need time before answering. Surprise is not the same as honesty.

never.point: Do not relabel pressure as patience
never.detail: Repeating a request every few days while calling it gentle persistence is still pressure. If you have asked and received a no or a not yet, say what you will do with that answer. Continuing to circle back without new information wears the other person down rather than persuading them.

never.point: Do not broker alone indefinitely
never.detail: If the other person will not put terms on the table, you can make one final clear request and then act on the answer. Endless solo negotiation, where you keep revising proposals nobody engages with, drains you and changes nothing. It is fair to name the impasse and decide what you will do next.

power_moves.name: The Shared Plane
power_moves.how_it_works: One person invests visible time and effort in a joint effort, which can make the other feel valued and also quietly obligated to reciprocate. The effect is goodwill mixed with a sense of debt. If a partner rearranges a whole weekend to help with your family event, thank them specifically and ask what would make the favor feel balanced rather than assumed.
power_moves.defense: Name the effort out loud and separate gratitude from obligation. You can say I really appreciate you giving up Saturday, and also I do not want you to feel I now owe you a matching favor. Ask directly what they expect. If the answer is nothing, trust it. If it is something specific, decide now whether you can offer it freely.

power_moves.name: The Named Council
power_moves.how_it_works: A promise gains force when a particular person or group is assigned to carry it. In a household, this can look like one partner declaring themselves the responsible one for bills or appointments and then citing that role when they want credit. The effect is that responsibility silently consolidates in one place.
power_moves.defense: Ask who else is on the council. If one person has quietly become the sole keeper of the budget, the calendar or the family logistics, propose a concrete split and a review date. You can say I want us both to know what is due and when, so let us divide these tasks and check in fortnightly.

power_moves.name: The Pre-Announcement Assembly
power_moves.how_it_works: Calling people together before a decision is made can build genuine buy-in or can function as a show of consultation after the direction is already set. In a relationship, a partner may gather everyone for a family meeting where the plan is presented as open. The effect is that objection feels rude.
power_moves.defense: Test the openness with one question. Ask what would have to change for this plan to look different. If the answer is nothing, the meeting was an announcement. You can respond by saying I need to think before I agree, and that is a complete answer. Ask for a day before any commitment is recorded.

power_moves.name: The Two-Signature Front
power_moves.how_it_works: Two people present a united proposal to a third party, which can look like solidarity but may mean one person's terms are carrying the pair. In a couple facing a landlord, an in-law or a school, one partner may speak for both with terms the other never fully approved. The effect is that the quieter person is bound by words they did not choose.
power_moves.defense: Agree before any joint meeting what each of you will and will not accept, and who speaks on which point. If your partner states a term you did not approve, you can say in the moment I need to pause, we have not settled that. Correcting a joint position in public is allowed and is not a betrayal.

power_moves.name: The Long Journey
power_moves.how_it_works: A large, visible gesture of effort, such as a long trip or an elaborate apology, can overshadow the smaller terms that still need agreeing. The effect is that the gesture absorbs the conversation and the original request goes unanswered. Grand effort can be sincere and still leave the practical question untouched.
power_moves.defense: Acknowledge the gesture, then return to the terms. You can say that meant a lot to me, and I still need to know whether we are splitting the rent this way from next month. Keep the practical question on the table until it has a clear answer. Effort and agreement are two separate matters.

leverage.detail: Choose a single concrete behavior you want, such as a weekly call or a shared chore on a set day. Ask for it plainly and let the other person answer. One named commitment is easier to test for follow-through than a broad promise of improvement, and it gives you a clear basis for deciding what to do next.

Agree to try a change for a fixed stretch, say a month, then review it together. A trial lowers the stakes for both people and makes it easier to say this is not working without treating the whole relationship as failed. Fix the review date at the start so neither of you has to raise it awkwardly.

Decide in advance what you will do if a term is not met, and tell the other person. For example, if plans keep getting cancelled without notice, you will stop holding the evening open. A stated limit is information, not a threat, and it lets the other person choose with full knowledge of the consequences.

Ask what they would need from you to feel the arrangement is fair, and listen without defending. Mutuality requires their conditions as well as yours. If they cannot name any, that itself is useful information, and you can say so kindly. A negotiation where only one side has stated terms is not yet a negotiation.

Do not dismantle your own supports, savings or friendships while a negotiation is unresolved. Having somewhere to go and people to call is not disloyalty. It is what lets you decline a bad deal calmly, and it keeps a no available to you even when the other person would prefer you had none.

closest.rationale: In May 2010 Lula flew to Tehran with Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan to seek a negotiated solution with President Ahmadinejad, framing the trip as a joint search for a negotiated settlement.

cousin.tell: Where a Co-Builder would share a decision jointly arrived at, Lula instead carried an offer to a third leader alongside a partner state, positioning himself as intermediary between Iran and outside powers.

basis.observation: He traveled personally alongside Erdogan to meet Ahmadinejad, framing the trip as a joint search for a negotiated solution to a conflict threatening regional stability.

sections.identity: Brazil's finance minister from 1993, Fernando Henrique Cardoso coordinated the Plano Real, whose transitional URV unit preceded the Real currency in July 1994.

matches.why: As finance minister Cardoso assembled economists to design the Plano Real. The program combined budget measures with an interim unit of account and a new currency, and its technical design was the work of a team.

pattern: The Plano Real unfolded in stages rather than at a single stroke. Public accounts were adjusted first, the Unidade Real de Valor then served as a transitional unit to realign prices, and the Real arrived on 1 July 1994. A team of economists worked under Cardoso's coordination. The method was one of announced stages, each checked before the next began.

On 4 May 2000, as president, Cardoso signed the Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal, which set public finance rules for fiscal responsibility. Note the shape of the measure: it governs how spending decisions are made, not any single spending decision. A household that agrees on who reviews the joint account each month is doing something similar in miniature, setting the method before the money moves.

Lei nº 9.313, signed on 13 November 1996, guaranteed free HIV and AIDS medication through the Sistema Único de Saúde. The Ministry of Health standardized drugs for each stage of infection and disease. The law reaches people through a structure that already existed, and the staging tells each patient what applies at their point. Commitments that name stages tend to survive contact with a changing situation.

In 2002 Cardoso issued a decree promulgating the Ushuaia Protocol on Democratic Commitment in Mercosur, Bolivia and Chile, ordering its full execution and compliance under Brazilian law. The step made an external agreement binding at home. Readers can borrow the modest version. When two people agree on something, writing down how it will be carried out and who will check turns a warm intention into a workable arrangement.

text: Listen for whether the other person describes how a decision would be made, or only what they want. Someone who says let's look at the budget together before booking the trip is offering a method. Someone who says I already booked it has presented an outcome. The first invites you to check along the way. The second asks you to react to something finished.

Notice sequencing in what people say about shared plans. A person who names the first step, the next step and how each will be checked is telling you they expect the arrangement to be reviewed. Listen also for who does the coordinating. If every stage is described in the passive voice, with no actor, ask plainly who is doing which part and by when.
examples: As finance minister from 1993, Fernando Henrique Cardoso assembled a team of economists and coordinated formulation of the Plano Real, which combined fiscal adjustment measures, created the Unidade Real de Valor as a transition unit, and introduced the Real currency on 1 July 1994.
On 4 May 2000, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed the Lei de Responsabilidade Fiscal, which established public finance rules for fiscal responsibility in Brazil.

Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed Lei nº 9.313 on 13 November 1996, which guaranteed free HIV and AIDS medication through the Sistema Único de Saúde, with the Ministry of Health standardizing drugs for each stage of infection and disease.

Fernando Henrique Cardoso, as Brazil's president, issued a decree in 2002 promulgating the Ushuaia Protocol on Democratic Commitment in Mercosur, Bolivia and Chile, ordering its full execution and compliance under Brazilian law.

spectrum.interested: Maya taped a receipt to the fridge and said she was trying a two-week grocery experiment, then added, “If that’s weird for you, say so.” Sam looked at the total circled in pencil and said, “I could try it.” That afternoon Sam texted a photo of the store’s weekly flyer, folded to the produce page, with no further message attached.
spectrum.invested: They began splitting the list on Sunday nights, each writing three dinners in a shared note. Sam bought a cheap scale; Maya printed a price-per-ounce chart and taped it beside the receipt. By Thursday, two jars of sauce sat unopened because both had checked the pantry first. The fridge shelf held labeled containers with dates written in marker, and the ledger showed a small surplus.
spectrum.done: On Saturday Maya said, “I’m not doing the ledger past this month.” Sam nodded and asked whether she wanted the chart taken down. She said leave it. Sam decided to keep tracking alone rather than press the point, and they agreed the next grocery run would be separate. Maya folded the receipt into her pocket, and Sam wrote down a shorter list.

works.detail: Before a joint purchase or trip, name the first step, who takes it and when you will look again. Say it back to each other once. A written two-line note on the fridge is enough. This lets a disagreement land on a stage rather than on a person.

works.point: Make the check small and regular
works.detail: Pick a fixed short conversation, perhaps ten minutes weekly, to check one agreement. Keep it narrow. Ask what changed since last time and what the next step is. Small regular checks catch drift earlier than one long reckoning after months.

When a shared task stalls, ask which of you is coordinating it and until when. A clear owner beats an assumption, and if neither wants it, split the task or drop it. Naming the coordinator is not a promotion; it comes with an end date.

works.point: Write the how, not just the what
works.detail: If you agree to save for something, add how you will track it and when you will review. Agreement on the purpose is warm. Agreement on the tracking is what survives a busy month. Keep the how short enough that you both remember it.

When a change is big, such as moving in or merging costs, set a defined interim arrangement with a review date. The Plano Real's URV worked this way for prices in the economy. Your version might be a shared spreadsheet for three months before anything is final.

never.point: Do not announce a finished decision
never.detail: Booking, signing or committing before the other person has agreed on the method invites a fight about the thing itself. Ask first whether you two should decide this together, and how. A finished outcome leaves the other person only the choice to accept or object.

never.point: Do not leave the check to guesswork
never.detail: An agreement with no review date drifts quietly. If you promised to look again, put the day somewhere you will both see it; a phone reminder is fine. The point is that checking is expected rather than suspicious.

never.point: Do not use a transition as a hiding place
never.detail: An interim arrangement needs an end. If a trial period keeps extending with no review, the other person cannot tell whether the trial is working or being avoided. Name the date the interim becomes permanent or gets dropped.

never.point: Do not treat a rule as a person
never.detail: A fiscal rule governs money; it does not describe anyone's character. Likewise, a household agreement about chores is not a verdict on who is kind. Keep the rule about the arrangement, so disagreements stay small and fixable.

never.point: Do not let one person carry every stage
never.detail: If you notice you are always the one proposing the sequence, ask directly whether the other person wants to own a stage. Their answer tells you something useful. If they decline every stage, that is information too, and you can decide what you are willing to keep offering.

power_moves.name: The staged rollout
power_moves.how_it_works: One person proposes handling a change in clearly named stages, with a check between each. It can feel reassuring, and it can also concentrate control with whoever names the stages, since they decide when a stage is complete.
power_moves.defense: Agree in advance what counts as each stage being done and who confirms it. A useful line: I like the sequence, and I want us both to say when stage one is finished. That keeps the method shared rather than held by one person.

power_moves.name: The rule instead of the outcome
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone reframes a dispute as a matter of fair procedure, which can lower the heat but also sidestep the actual request. You may end up arguing about the process while the original need goes unaddressed.
power_moves.defense: Welcome the rule and then return to the request once. A useful question is what we want to happen after the rule is agreed. If the process talk keeps replacing the answer, say so plainly and ask for a date.

power_moves.name: The transitional phase
power_moves.how_it_works: A temporary unit or trial period lets people adjust before a permanent change, and it can also let one person delay indefinitely. The risk is a trial that quietly becomes the living arrangement.
power_moves.defense: Set the trial's review date when you start it. One way to say it: let us try this for six weeks and decide on the twentieth. Write the date down. If it passes without review, raise it yourself without accusation.

power_moves.name: The binding step
power_moves.how_it_works: Turning an intention into a recorded commitment can make it dependable, and it can also be used to lock in an agreement the other person was still considering. The moment of formalizing carries weight.
power_moves.defense: Before any formal step, ask whether you are both ready or one of you needs more time. Slowing down is allowed. Asking whether to confirm this next week instead protects both people from a decision made in momentum.

power_moves.name: The coordination claim
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone says they are handling the arrangements and asks you not to worry, which can be generous and can also remove your view from decisions that affect you. Later you learn what was decided for you.
power_moves.defense: Accept help and keep one point of visibility. Ask to see the plan before it is final. A line that works here: thank you, send me the list before you book anything. Generosity and transparency can live in the same arrangement.

leverage.detail: You can ask how a shared decision will be made before agreeing to it. A test for mutuality is whether the other person offers a method and welcomes your edits. If they only want your yes, that tells you where the decision sits.

You can choose a date to revisit any agreement, including ones you proposed. A test is whether the other person shows up to the review or finds reasons to postpone. One postponement is ordinary. A pattern is information you can act on.

leverage.point: Decline a stage you did not agree to
leverage.detail: You can say no to a step that arrived without your input, even a kind one. A test for mutuality is how the other person responds to a calm no. Acceptance and a new question are good signs; pressure or sulking is a sign to slow down.

You can state which parts of a shared plan you will coordinate and which you will not. A test is whether the split holds for a month. If you end up quietly carrying their part, revisit the split rather than silently absorbing it.

leverage.point: Leave the interim when it stalls
leverage.detail: You can decide that a trial with no end is not working for you. A test is whether the other person will set a real date when asked. If not, you can step back from the arrangement with a plain explanation and no ultimatum.

closest.rationale: As finance minister Cardoso assembled economists to design the Plano Real. The program combined budget measures with an interim unit of account and a new currency, and its technical design was the work of a team.

cousin.tell: A proceduralist might agree in advance how competing plans would be chosen. Cardoso’s role here was assembling specialists to develop the plan itself and letting their technical work shape its contents.

basis.style: Sharing the design of Brazil’s currency transition
basis.observation: Cardoso coordinated the group while serving under President Itamar Franco. Its members designed a sequence of changes that let people compare prices in a common unit before exchanging their money for reais.

sections.identity: Costa Rican president Óscar Arias Sánchez authored the Esquipulas II peace plan setting reciprocal commitments for Central America's five governments.

matches.why: Arias drafted Esquipulas II laying out reciprocal commitments — ceasefire, free elections, press freedom and amnesty — a plan submitted to Central America's five governments, who had to accept and sign it jointly.

pattern: Esquipulas II put a ceasefire, free elections, press freedom, civil liberties and amnesty for political prisoners into a single package presented to five governments. Each side's commitments were bound to the others rather than handed down to one party. Whether or not you admire the content, the structure is legible: a proposal that only works if everyone signs the same page. In a relationship, that shape shows up when two people write down what each will do, together, and check it before anything starts.

The Arms Trade Treaty proposal was presented at the 61st United Nations General Assembly in September 2006 on behalf of seven sponsoring states. It was a shared public ask, not a private request. Notice the discipline of a position that several parties could stand behind without erasing their differences. A partner who can state a wish aloud, in plain words, and still leave room for your answer is offering something sturdier than a hint dropped once and never repeated.

In June 2007 the decision to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China was announced at Casa Presidencial alongside the foreign minister. It was a consequential shift made publicly, with a named second voice. Whatever one thinks of the move, the form matters: change disclosed rather than discovered. In ordinary life the parallel is modest. If a decision reshapes a shared calendar, telling the other person before it lands is basic courtesy, not confession.

A 2007 electoral amparo filed by Deputy Óscar López Arias with the Supreme Electoral Tribunal challenged the president and other officials over constitutional claims tied to the signing of the free trade agreement. Contest through an available channel, with a stated grievance, rather than quiet erosion. Couples rarely have tribunals, but they do have the option of naming a disagreement once, clearly, and letting the other person respond. Repeated low-grade sniping is a different animal from one clean objection.

text: Listen for whether the other person describes an agreement as something the two of you made together or as something they decided and announced. The first leaves room for your answer. The second treats your assent as a formality. Ask directly, in your own words, what they think you agreed to, and notice whether their account matches yours. A mismatch is information, not an accusation.

Pay attention to how they handle a no. A proposal offered jointly should survive a declined clause. If every hesitation is treated as obstruction, the mutuality was decorative. You might say, I want to look at this part before we lock it in. What happens next tells you more than the original offer did.
examples: Óscar Arias Sánchez drafted the peace plan known as Esquipulas II, which set out a ceasefire, free elections, press freedom and civil liberties, and amnesty for political prisoners. The plan was submitted to Central America's five governments, which had to accept and sign it jointly.

In 2007, Deputy Óscar López Arias filed an electoral amparo with the Supreme Electoral Tribunal against President Óscar Arias Sánchez and other officials, alleging constitutional violations in the signing of the Dominican Republic–Central America–United States Free Trade Agreement (TLC).

On 19 September 2006, Costa Rican President Óscar Arias presented the proposed Arms Trade Treaty at the 61st United Nations General Assembly, speaking on behalf of the sponsoring states: Costa Rica, Argentina, Australia, Finland, Japan, Kenya and the United Kingdom.

On 6 June 2007, President Óscar Arias Sánchez and Foreign Minister Bruno Stagno Ugarte announced at Casa Presidencial Costa Rica's decision to normalize its ties with the People's Republic of China by establishing diplomatic relations.

spectrum.interested: Maya texted her brother, “I’d be open to coffee, but no pressure. If you’d rather not, just say so and I’ll leave it.” She named a Saturday diner near the bus depot and added that he could pick the time or suggest another place. The message ended without a question mark, letting silence count as an answer.
spectrum.invested: Two days later he replied with a photo of the diner’s laminated menu and wrote, “Thursday at six works. I’ll get there early and grab the booth by the window.” Maya confirmed she would bring the folder of their mother’s insurance letters. They agreed to keep the first hour to logistics, then decide whether to order pie.
spectrum.done: At the table he said, “I can talk about the letters, but I’m not ready to discuss Dad.” Maya nodded, slid the folder across, and said she would mail copies instead of pushing. She can still invite him to the next meeting; if he declines, she can send one line wishing him well and stop there.

works.detail: Take one recurring friction, such as weekend plans or money, and put each person's commitment in a shared note. Read it back to each other. If one side's column stays empty, you have learned something before resentment sets in.

When a decision affects both of you, discuss it with the person present rather than announcing it after. A simple heads-up before the fact costs little and prevents the discovery that someone else already knew.
Say what bothers you in a couple of sentences and let the other person answer. A single clear complaint is easier to respond to than a string of hints spread over weeks.

works.point: Ask what they heard you agree to
works.detail: After a big conversation, invite them to summarize it. Differences in the summaries are normal. What matters is whether both of you can correct the record without a fight.
When you propose something, include a part you are genuinely unsure about. A partner who can sit with that uncertainty is telling you they want agreement, not applause.

never.point: Do not present a decision as a done deal
never.detail: Announcing a choice that reshapes shared time and then asking for thoughts inverts the order. The other person is left ratifying rather than deciding, and they will notice.

never.point: Do not treat a no as a negotiation tactic
never.detail: If every hesitation gets answered with pressure, the offer was never mutual. Accept the decline, ask what would help, and let the next move be theirs.

never.point: Do not file the same complaint repeatedly
never.detail: Raising the same grievance every week wears down the listener without resolving anything. One clear statement, a response, and then a decision about what you will do next are enough.

never.point: Do not build a package that only benefits you
never.detail: A joint plan where all the costs land on one person is a demand wearing a treaty's clothes. Check the columns honestly before presenting anything.

never.point: Do not let a public gesture substitute for private follow-through
never.detail: A grand statement in front of friends is not the same as showing up on a Tuesday. Watch the ordinary weeks, not the announcement.

power_moves.name: The package deal
power_moves.how_it_works: They bundle several commitments into one take-it-or-leave-it offer, so a small hesitation feels like rejecting everything. The effect can be paralysis or a rushed yes you later regret.
power_moves.defense: Separate the bundle. Say, I can agree to the first and third parts and I need to think about the second. A fair offer survives being taken apart.

power_moves.name: The public announcement
power_moves.how_it_works: A plan is revealed in front of others, making objection socially costly. You may feel cornered into agreement.
power_moves.defense: You can say, warmly and in front of the group, that sounds good and I want to talk it through when it is just us. Then do that.

power_moves.name: The named second voice
power_moves.how_it_works: They cite a friend or relative who supposedly agrees with them, lending weight to a request. This can make your hesitation look like the odd position.
power_moves.defense: Ask what you yourself think, not what the third party thinks. You might say, I hear that they are on board. I am still deciding for me.

power_moves.name: The formal objection
power_moves.how_it_works: They raise one crisp complaint with dates and details, which can feel like a courtroom rather than a conversation. The precision may leave you defensive.
power_moves.defense: Take a breath and answer the substance rather than the tone. You can say, I want to respond to the specific point. Give me a day to think.

power_moves.name: The quiet shift
power_moves.how_it_works: A consequential change gets made with minimal discussion, and the reasoning arrives later as explanation. You discover the new arrangement after it is settled.
power_moves.defense: Name the gap without drama. I would rather hear about a change before it happens. Can we agree on that going forward? Then watch whether it holds.

leverage.detail: No joint agreement is binding on you until you actually accept it. Read the terms, ask questions, and use your own words to say yes. A plan that cannot survive your scrutiny was never a shared plan.
You can raise a disagreement once, plainly, and then decide what you will do based on the response. The reply is the test, and afterward the choice is yours, not theirs to delay.

Shared time is a resource you allocate. Before agreeing to a standing arrangement, check whether the hours actually work for you. If they do not, saying so early is kinder than silent resentment later.

Ask directly, in plain words, what they are committing to and when. Compare their answer with what you are offering. Uneven columns are worth discussing before anything is signed, verbally or otherwise.
You can decline to continue a negotiation that stops being reciprocal. Leaving is not a threat. You might say, I do not think we are landing this, and I am going to step back for now.

closest.rationale: Arias drafted Esquipulas II laying out reciprocal commitments — ceasefire, free elections, press freedom and amnesty — a plan submitted to Central America's five governments, who had to accept and sign it jointly.

cousin.tell: Where a Bridge Builder would seat rival delegations face to face, Arias wrote a single package of mutual undertakings and sought each president's signature on it.

basis.observation: The plan ties each government's commitments together rather than imposing terms on one side; Arias framed it as a shared package the five presidents had to adopt, not a unilateral demand.

sections.identity: Venezuelan independence leader whose 1815 Jamaica Letter reframed the case for Spanish American independence around local conditions and British interests.

matches.why: In the Jamaica Letter of 6 September 1815, Bolívar recast Spanish American independence around local conditions and circumstances, arguing for British support through that reframing rather than a simple plea.

pattern: The Jamaica Letter of 6 September 1815 does something you can watch for in any stubborn conversation. Written in Kingston to a British reader, Henry Cullen of Falmouth, it starts from the situation of the American provinces rather than from grievance alone. It asks what form of government those circumstances could actually sustain, then what a British reader might do. The move is a reframe, and it gives the listener a role in the answer.

Before the Angostura congress on 15 February 1819, the speech was drafted in late 1818 and shown to Manuel Palacio Fajardo for comment. That sequence matters more than the rhetoric. A position was formed, written down, handed to someone else, and only then delivered. If you want to know whether a partner treats your view as real, watch whether they let you see a draft of their thinking before it hardens into a decision.

The convocation issued in Lima on 7 December 1824, two days before Ayacucho, invited five governments to send plenipotentiaries to Panama. Note the timing. An invitation went out while the outcome was still uncertain, not after the result was safely banked. The invitation was also specific about who was asked and where they would meet. Vague enthusiasm costs nothing. A named invitation with a date asks something of the person making it.

The Decreto de Guerra a Muerte, issued at Trujillo on 15 June 1813, declared war to the death after the First Republic fell. It is the hardest item in this record, and it is not a model for resolving a disagreement over dinner. What it shows plainly is that extreme language sets a course that is difficult to walk back. Words that foreclose options tend to be remembered long after the feeling that produced them has passed.

text: Listen for whether the other person asks what your circumstances can sustain or only what they want from you. A question shaped around your situation, your hours and your obligations sounds different from a request dressed as concern. The Kingston letter works because it reasons from conditions on the ground. In conversation, that sounds like someone checking the shape of your week before proposing a plan.

Listen also for the difference between a position delivered and a position shared. Someone who shows you the draft, the half-formed version, is inviting your comment while it can still change something. Someone who arrives with the conclusion fixed and asks only for agreement is doing something else. You can say so plainly: "I would rather hear this before it is settled."
examples: On 6 September 1815, while in Kingston, Jamaica, Simón Bolívar wrote a letter addressed to a British subject, later identified as Henry Cullen of Falmouth, setting out his arguments for Latin American independence and seeking British support.

On 15 February 1819, Simón Bolívar delivered a speech at the Second Constituent Congress of Venezuela in Angostura, addressing the congressmen on the constitutional project and Venezuela's situation, a text he had drafted in late 1818 and shown to Manuel Palacio Fajardo for comment.

As head of state of Peru, Simón Bolívar issued a convocation on 7 December 1824 in Lima, two days before the Battle of Ayacucho, inviting the governments of Gran Colombia, Mexico, Río de la Plata, Chile and Central America to install an assembly of plenipotentiaries in Panama.

On 15 June 1813 in Trujillo, Simón Bolívar issued the Decreto de Guerra a Muerte, a proclamation declaring war to the death against royalist forces in Venezuela following the fall of the First Republic.

spectrum.interested: Maya slides the neighbour’s sourdough schedule across the counter and says, “I could try Saturday, or leave it if that’s easier.” She keeps her hand off the paper, waiting. Then she adds, “If you’re in, I’ll bring the jar of starter. If not, no problem.” Nothing more is promised, and the plan stays optional for both of them.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday there are two jars in the fridge, one labelled with tape. They agree on a time and split the shopping: flour from the corner shop, a spare loaf tin borrowed and returned. One of them texts a photo of a bubbly starter. Concrete choices start appearing: who carries what, where it cools, when it’s checked.
spectrum.done: On Saturday morning one says, “Actually, I’m out on this. I’ll leave the tin by the door.” The other can reply plainly, “Understood, thanks.” Then comes a choice: bake alone, ask someone else, or set the jar aside. A stated limit is just information, and respecting it means no follow-up text, no second attempt, and no reading into the silence.

works.point: Ask what the situation can bear
works.detail: Before proposing anything, name the constraint out loud, the shift, the family obligation, the tired Tuesday. Then ask what fits. This mirrors the Jamaica Letter's starting point and saves you from planning around an imaginary week.

If a decision involves both of you, show it early and half-formed. Say, "This is not settled; tell me what I am missing." A partner who comments usefully is working with you rather than waiting to react.

Name the day, the place and what you are asking. A concrete invitation is easier to accept and easier to decline. Vagueness protects the asker and burdens the asked, which is why specific plans sort people faster.

works.point: Watch the timing of a yes
works.detail: Notice whether agreement arrives before or after the hard part is mentioned. Someone who commits while the outcome is uncertain is telling you something a later yes cannot. Ask for the early version when it matters.

works.point: Keep the exit open in your own words
works.detail: When you are upset, say what happened and what you want next. Avoid language that closes every door. If you have already closed one, reopen it explicitly and say you spoke too broadly. Repair is a choice you can make first.

never.point: Do not reframe to dodge
never.detail: Reframing is not winning by rewording. If your partner names a real problem, restating it as something else avoids the point. Ask, "Is this still the same issue?" before you try a new angle.

never.point: Do not share a draft as a trap
never.detail: Showing your thinking early invites comment. If you then treat every comment as an attack, you have used openness as a test. Say plainly whether you want feedback or reassurance before the conversation starts.

never.point: Do not send a vague invitation and grade the reply
never.detail: An unspecific ask that you secretly measure against a hoped-for answer is unfair. If you want Thursday, say Thursday. Give the other person a fair chance to say yes or no to something real.

never.point: Do not match harsh words with harsher
never.detail: When a conversation turns heated, escalating language rarely produces clarity. Step out and name it. Try, "I am too wound up to do this well; can we pick it up at eight?" Then actually pick it up.

never.point: Do not treat early enthusiasm as a settlement
never.detail: Warmth in the first weeks is not a contract. Reading commitment into it and then resenting the gap is a way to suffer twice. Let the early version stay early and let later actions update your view.

power_moves.name: The reframe that assigns a role
power_moves.how_it_works: One person restates the problem from the other's position and then asks for a specific contribution. This can open a stuck conversation by giving the listener something to do. It can also slide into managing the other person's choices for them.
power_moves.defense: If someone reframes your problem and hands you a role, you can say, "That is a useful way to put it, but I want to decide what I do." Accept the new angle and keep the decision. If you are the one reframing, offer the role and leave the answer open.

power_moves.name: The early draft
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone shares a plan before it is final, inviting comment while change is still possible. This signals trust and can produce better decisions. It can also invite endless revisions, or become a way to say you were consulted when you were not.
power_moves.defense: Ask what stage this is at and what comment is actually welcome. Try, "Is this still open to change, or are you telling me the plan?" If it is open, name the one thing you would change and let the rest go.

power_moves.name: The timed invitation
power_moves.how_it_works: An invitation is issued while matters are uncertain, naming who is asked and where they would meet. It can show seriousness because it costs the asker something before the result is known. It can also pressure an answer before the other person is ready.
power_moves.defense: You are allowed to say, I cannot answer that today, I need until Sunday. A deadline set by the asker is not automatically your deadline. Offer a real time you will respond and keep it.

power_moves.name: The foreclosing phrase
power_moves.how_it_works: Strong words settle a course quickly when someone is hurt or cornered. They can feel like clarity in the moment. They often remove options that the speaker later wants back, and the other person remembers the words after the mood has gone.
power_moves.defense: If you hear a phrase that closes everything, respond to the feeling before the wording. Try, "That sounded final; do you mean it as final?" If you said it, correct it early and specifically rather than hoping it fades.

power_moves.name: The concrete ask
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone replaces a general wish with a named request, a day, a place, a thing to do. It makes agreement possible and refusal honest. It can still be an ask disguised as a decision already taken, which is where clarity turns into pressure.
power_moves.defense: Check whether you are being asked or told. If it is an ask, you can decline without a long explanation and still keep the relationship warm. Say, not this Thursday, and offer another day if you want one.

leverage.detail: Before any negotiation, say the one thing that cannot move this week. You choose what that is. A partner who works with it has passed a real test, and one who ignores it has told you something useful without any argument.

You can request to see a plan before it is final. Say, "I would like to hear this while it can still change." If the answer is no, you have learned how decisions will be made, which is information you can act on.
When an invitation or a difficult question arrives, name when you will answer. This keeps the pace yours without stonewalling. Then answer at that time with a plain yes, no or a specific alternative.

Name one modest need and watch whether it changes anything within a week. This is not a test of love but a test of follow-through. If nothing shifts, decide whether to ask again or to stop asking; both are yours to choose.

leverage.point: Decide what a harsh phrase means
leverage.detail: If strong words have been said, ask once whether they stand. You can accept an apology and still name the boundary. You can also end the conversation and return when both of you can speak with room to move.

closest.rationale: In the Jamaica Letter of 6 September 1815, Bolívar recast Spanish American independence around local conditions and circumstances, arguing for British support through that reframing rather than a simple plea.

cousin.tell: Where a Bridge Builder would have seated Britain and the American provinces at one table, Bolívar instead wrote to a single British subject, restructuring the argument so Cullen would reach the conclusion on his own.

basis.style: Argument reframed for a British reader
basis.observation: Written in Kingston to Henry Cullen of Falmouth, the letter reasons from the situation of the American provinces, asking what form of government their circumstances could sustain and what a British reader might do.

sections.identity: José de San Martín, as Protector of Peru, issued the Ley de vientres, decreeing freedom from slavery for those born from 28 July 1821 onward.

matches.why: As Protector of Peru he issued the Ley de vientres, a norm already tried in Buenos Aires, freeing from slavery those born from 28 July 1821 onward, days after independence.

pattern: A continental plan took shape by 1814 that avoided an offensive from Upper Peru and instead concentrated forces in Chile, carried out through the Andes crossing of 1817. The choice was logistical and patient, a refusal to spend strength where the ground favored the defender. In ordinary terms, it is the decision to stop arguing about the same locked door and put the effort where change can actually happen.

On 25 July 1821, a bando issued in Lima announced that the solemn proclamation of independence would take place on Saturday the 28th and asked the noble vecindario to attend the oath and to adorn and illuminate their houses on the nights of Friday, Saturday and Sunday. The notice fixed the date and made participation visible. A clear invitation with a time and a task gives people something concrete to accept or decline.

After the Guayaquil interview of July 1822, an irrevocable resignation was presented on 20 September before the first Constituent Congress held at the University of San Marcos. The step put the decision in a formal body rather than in a private arrangement. When a role has run its course, handing the matter to an agreed process can be cleaner than prolonging a negotiation that no longer fits.

As Protector of Peru, San Martín issued the Ley de vientres, a Buenos Aires measure he applied in Peru days after independence, freeing from slavery those born from 28 July 1821 onward. The Protectorate decree power, rather than the army, put the freedom into law on a fixed date. That is advocacy in its plainest form: ask the person who can change things for something specific on someone else’s behalf.

text: Listen for a stated date and a named action. The bando did not ask for a general mood of loyalty. It asked people to attend an oath and light their houses on three named nights. In conversation, a partner who says what will happen and when is easier to trust than one who describes a feeling without a shape.

Listen for the difference between a request and a demand. The bando asked the vecindario to attend, and it made the request public. A partner can ask you to show up for something specific without turning your answer into a test of character. By the same token, you can say yes, say no, or ask what the occasion actually requires.
examples: In 1814 José de San Martín finished shaping a continental plan that avoided an offensive from Upper Peru and instead concentrated forces in Chile, the strategic scheme carried out through the Andes crossing of 1817.

On 25 July 1821, José de San Martín issued a bando in Lima announcing to Peruvians that the solemn proclamation of independence would take place on Saturday the 28th, and asking the noble vecindario to attend the oath, adorn and illuminate its houses on the nights of Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
After the Guayaquil interview of July 1822, San Martín presented his irrevocable resignation on 20 September before the first Constituent Congress held at the University of San Marcos.
As Protector of Peru, José de San Martín issued the so-called "Ley de vientres," a legal norm that had given good results in Buenos Aires and freed from slavery those born from 28 July 1821 onward.

spectrum.interested: At the community garden shed, Mira slides the clipboard across the potting bench but keeps her hand flat on it. "I could take over the seed inventory if that suits you—or leave it with Jo, honestly." She names two dates she's free. The other person can pick either, counter, or hand it back without awkwardness. Nothing is signed; the clipboard sits between them.
spectrum.invested: By Thursday, the other volunteer texts a photo of the seed packets sorted into labeled envelopes on their kitchen table, asking whether the tomato rows should be alphabetical or by planting month. Mira replies with a marked-up list and offers to meet Saturday at nine. They agree on the shed, bring their own pens, and split the labeling work without discussing who will stay longer.
spectrum.done: Saturday, the other volunteer says plainly, "I can finish these envelopes, but I won't take the March market shift—I'm done after this box." Mira nods, writes their name only on the inventory line, and asks who else might cover the market. She can accept the limit, adjust the roster, or step back herself. A slow reply is just a slow reply, not a verdict.

works.detail: Say what you will do and when, the way the bando named Saturday the 28th. A concrete evening and a concrete task are easier to answer than a vague hope to spend more time together. If the date no longer works, change it out loud rather than letting it fade.

works.point: Ask the person who can act
works.detail: The Ley de vientres went through the Protectorate decree, not the army. In a shared household, ask the person who actually controls the calendar or the account. Skip the intermediaries. State the specific change you want and let them answer for it directly.

The Buenos Aires norm had already produced results before it traveled to Peru. When you propose a fix at home, point to something that worked elsewhere. A borrowed arrangement is easier to discuss than an untested theory, and it gives both of you a shared reference.

The resignation went before the Constituent Congress rather than staying a private conversation. If a role or arrangement is over, say so to the person or group that needs to hear it. A short written note can prevent months of ambiguous messages and reopen space for both people.

The 1814 plan stopped pressing Upper Peru and moved effort to Chile. At home, notice which argument keeps returning without movement. Try putting the same energy into one smaller, reachable decision. A solved practical question often does more for a relationship than another round on the old ground.

never.point: Never issue a decree about someone else’s life
never.detail: The Protectorate power was public and legal. In a partnership, do not announce a change that governs the other person’s time, money or family without their agreement. Ask first. A decision that lands on someone without their yes is not a shared plan.

never.point: Never mistake a public date for consent
never.detail: The bando invited the vecindario to attend the oath. Attendance was still an answer. Do not treat an invitation you made as proof that your partner agreed to anything beyond it. Wait for their reply, and accept a no without renegotiating the date.

never.point: Never use a resignation as a threat
never.detail: The resignation was presented once and called irrevocable. Do not borrow that weight to win an argument. Saying you are done as a way to force a reaction turns a real ending into leverage. If you mean to leave, say so clearly. If you do not, say what you actually need.

never.point: Never skip the person who can change things
never.detail: The Ley de vientres went through the authority that could enact it. In a dispute with a partner, do not route your request through friends or relatives and hope it arrives. Speak to the person themselves. Going around them breeds confusion and invites others into a decision that belongs between you.

never.point: Never let an old plan override a new fact
never.detail: The 1814 scheme changed when the ground changed. Do not keep defending a household arrangement out of loyalty to how you first set it up. If circumstances have shifted, say what is different now. A plan that cannot be revised becomes a source of quiet resentment.

power_moves.name: The fixed invitation
power_moves.how_it_works: You name a time and an action, as the bando named Saturday the 28th and the three illuminated nights. The other person can accept, decline, or propose another date. The invitation is clear, and the answer stays theirs to give.
power_moves.defense: If a fixed invitation feels like pressure, say so plainly. “I can do Saturday, but I won’t promise the whole weekend.” You can accept part of it, ask for a different time, or say no. A real invitation survives a real answer.

power_moves.name: The duty bearer
power_moves.how_it_works: You take your request to the person who can actually change the situation, as the Protectorate decree carried the Ley de vientres into law. You do not ask a friend to ask your partner. You say what you want to the person with the power to grant or refuse it.
power_moves.defense: When someone asks you to speak for them to a third person, you can decline. “That conversation belongs between you two.” You are not a messenger service, and carrying their request can put you in the middle of a decision you did not make. If you choose to help, you can do so as a witness at a conversation between them, not as a replacement for it.

power_moves.name: The borrowed precedent
power_moves.how_it_works: You point to a measure that worked elsewhere, as the Buenos Aires norm preceded the Peruvian law. The precedent gives the discussion a shape. “My sister and her partner do the calendar this way” is a starting offer, not a verdict on your household.
power_moves.defense: If a precedent is used to shut down your objection, you can say it does not fit your situation. “That worked for them, but our weeks are different.” You are allowed to test the borrowed idea against your own facts and reject it.

power_moves.name: The formal close
power_moves.how_it_works: You put an ending before the group or person that needs to receive it, as the resignation went before the Constituent Congress. The move ends ambiguity. It does not reopen the same negotiation under a new heading.
power_moves.defense: If someone declares an arrangement over without hearing you, you can ask for the terms in writing. “Send me the date and what changes.” You may accept the ending or ask for one more conversation. You are not required to agree on the spot.

power_moves.name: The concentrated effort
power_moves.how_it_works: You stop spending on a front that will not move and put the effort where it can, as the 1814 plan turned from Upper Peru toward Chile. You choose one reachable decision and give it real attention. The rest can wait without becoming a betrayal.
power_moves.defense: If a partner calls your focus a withdrawal, you can name the smaller decision and why it matters. “I’m not leaving the rest, I’m finishing this one thing first.” You can offer a date for the next piece, or ask them to take one piece themselves.

leverage.point: Set the date, keep the answer
leverage.detail: Propose one evening and one shared task, as the bando proposed attendance on a named Saturday. Ask your partner if that works. Their reply, yes or no, is information you can use. Do not treat the invitation as a commitment they already made.

If something in the household needs to change, ask the person who can change it. Say what you want in one or two sentences. If they say they need time, name a day to return to it. You can also decide the request is not worth pursuing and drop it openly.

Suggest a small arrangement for two weeks, the way a tried measure gets a trial. “We each take one school run this week. If it’s awful, we stop.” A time limit lets both of you test the fit without a permanent promise. Review it on the day you set.

When a conversation circles, ask for the specific terms in a message. “So we’re saying Friday, not the weekend.” A short written summary is easy to check. It also shows whether the other person agrees with the version you heard. You can correct it before anything changes.

Name the single decision you want to settle this month and leave the rest for later. Tell your partner which one and why. If they push for everything at once, you can say the other items are not on the table yet. Focus is a choice you make, not a verdict on them.

closest.rationale: As Protector of Peru he issued the Ley de vientres, a norm already tried in Buenos Aires, freeing from slavery those born from 28 July 1821 onward, days after independence.

cousin.tell: Unlike an Open Book who says it, means it, does it, San Martín signed a dated decree freeing children born from 28 July 1821, a concrete remedy on paper rather than a transparent personal stance.

basis.observation: He took a Buenos Aires measure and applied it in Peru days after independence, using his Protectorate decree power rather than his army, so the freedom landed in law on a fixed date.

sections.identity: Cuban independence leader José Martí drafted and co-signed the Montecristi Manifesto with Máximo Gómez on 25 March 1895.

matches.why: Martí drafted the Montecristi Manifesto and signed it with Máximo Gómez on 25 March 1895, so the text carried two signatures rather than one man's pledge alone.

pattern: A signed page shows who stayed at the table until the final line. When two people put their names under the same words, neither can later claim the other wrote it alone. Watch for the second signature in any joint effort. A partner who adds a name to a shared plan accepts a share of the blame if it fails, and that is heavier than praise for a draft only one person carries.

Founding Patria in New York in 1892 gave Martí a way to keep people in touch between meetings and public speeches. In its opening issue he identified unity as part of the newspaper’s purpose. In your own life, a shared place to write plans down can do more than another promise to communicate better. It only works if both people can add an item and see it answered.

An essay can travel. “Nuestra América” appeared in New York in January 1891 and was printed again in Mexico weeks later. Put a thought into the world and it may reach readers you never meet. The same holds for how a partner speaks about you when you are absent. A private promise and a public description should match. When they diverge, notice which version gets repeated.

A speech honoring young men killed twenty years earlier can be a way of saying the past still has weight. Speaking at the Liceo Cubano in Tampa in November 1891, Martí addressed a room gathered to remember. Consider how a partner treats anniversaries and losses that predate you. Someone who makes room for your earlier grief tells you something about how they hold history, including the parts they did not cause.

text: Listen for names. Someone who drafted a joint text and signed alongside another person knows how to say we. In conversation, notice whether a partner speaks of shared decisions as shared, or quietly recasts every agreement as their own idea. The wording is small. The habit behind it grows.

Listen for the second printing. When something you said in private comes back to you in public, check whether it survived the trip intact. A partner who repeats your view to friends in a form you would recognize is doing careful work. A partner who sharpens it into something you never said is doing something else.
examples: José Martí published his essay "Nuestra América" on 10 January 1891 in the New York Revista Ilustrada, with a second printing on 30 January 1891 in El Partido Liberal of Mexico.
In 1892 Martí founded Patria in New York. In its first issue he presented the newspaper as a place to bring supporters of Cuban independence together and give their organizing a common voice.

spectrum.interested: At the card shop counter, one person slides a blank card toward the other and says, "I drafted something—change anything or write your own." They leave the pen between them, not in anyone's hand. The draft is short, signed with one name and a question mark. Nothing is promised. The other can add a line, cross out a sentence, or simply say the card works as it is.
spectrum.invested: Two days later the card comes back with a crossed-out phrase, a replacement in different ink, and both names printed side by side at the bottom. They compare the ribbon choice at the till: navy or cream. One suggests cream to match the envelope; the other agrees but keeps the receipt. The gift sits on the table, wrapped, with the card tucked inside but not yet sealed.
spectrum.done: On Friday one says, "I'd rather not sign this one—I'll give a separate card." They set their pen down. The other can say, "Understood," hand back the unsigned card, and decide whether to sign alone, ask someone else, or leave the note out entirely. A clear no is enough. The next move belongs to whoever holds the card now.

works.detail: Before committing to a shared plan, ask directly who else is putting their name to it. A plain question such as “Is this ours, or mine with your approval?” settles the matter in one sentence. You learn quickly whether the other person intends to carry the weight with you.

works.point: Let the small deadline be the test
works.detail: Suggest something routine and repeatable: a weekly call, a standing walk. The first one is easy. The third or fourth shows what holds. Ask yourself whether the effort came from both sides without a reminder, and say so out loud if the pattern is lopsided.

Ask a friend how your partner describes the relationship when you are not there. You are not gathering evidence for a trial. You are checking whether the private and public accounts are the same document. If they differ, ask your partner about the gap in plain language.

When your partner mentions an old loss or an anniversary, make room for it even if it predates you. Offer to be present, or ask what they would prefer. Treating the past as real, rather than as competition, is a small act that tends to be returned.

Stay involved in the work and friendships that exist outside the relationship. A person with a full week is easier to be honest with. Say what you need for that outside life, and expect the same courtesy in return.

never.point: Never sign what you have not read
never.detail: If a shared plan arrives already decided, slow down. Ask for the terms in your own words before you agree. Signing to keep the peace puts your name on choices you did not make, and that is hard to undo later.

never.point: Never mistake one speech for a record
never.detail: A single moving evening does not establish a pattern. Notice what happens on ordinary Tuesdays. If you find yourself measuring the relationship by its best hour, add up the rest of the week before drawing conclusions.

never.point: Never let the deadline pass in silence
never.detail: When something you agreed to goes unmet, say it plainly and soon. “We said Thursday and it is now Sunday” is enough. Swallowing the disappointment teaches you both that the agreement was optional.

never.point: Never edit your own message to match theirs
never.detail: If your partner recasts your words in public, correct the record gently and without drama. Your view is yours to state. Adjusting it to fit their version, over and over, slowly erases the person they claimed to want.

never.point: Never treat the cause as a rival
never.detail: Work that matters to your partner will take time and attention. Ask for a schedule rather than a choice between you and it. If the schedule never leaves room for you, that is the fact to discuss, not the work itself.

power_moves.name: The Unread Draft
power_moves.how_it_works: Someone presents a decision as already settled and invites you to agree. The apparent courtesy of being consulted hides the fact that the terms were fixed without you.
power_moves.defense: Ask for the details in plain words and take a day before answering. A simple “Send me the version you want me to agree to and I will reply tomorrow” keeps the choice yours. If the reply is impatience, that tells you something about how future decisions will go.

power_moves.name: The Solo Credit
power_moves.how_it_works: A shared effort gets retold as one person's achievement. You notice your contribution missing from the account, and correcting it feels petty.
power_moves.defense: Say it once, lightly: “We did that part together.” If it keeps happening, raise the pattern when you are both calm and ask whether your name belongs on the next one. You are entitled to know where you stand before you invest more.

power_moves.name: The Old Wound
power_moves.how_it_works: A past hurt gets invoked to explain present behavior, and you are expected to absorb the cost. Sympathy for the history turns into permission for the current habit.
power_moves.defense: Offer care and keep your boundary. “I am sorry that happened, and I still need us to agree on this” can hold both truths at once. If the history becomes a reason you never get a straight answer, name that aloud.

power_moves.name: The Public Version
power_moves.how_it_works: What your partner says about you to others is warmer, or colder, than what they say to your face. You hear the difference secondhand and start doubting your own reading.
power_moves.defense: Ask about it directly rather than through a friend: “I heard you described us this way. Is that how you see it?” Their answer, more than the original remark, shows whether the two versions can be brought back together.

power_moves.name: The Forever Cause
power_moves.how_it_works: A large commitment, work or family or a long project, becomes the standing reason that small promises slip. The cause is real, which makes any complaint feel small.
power_moves.defense: Separate the cause from the calendar. Ask for one protected hour and see whether it holds. “I am not asking you to drop it. I am asking for Thursday.” If even that cannot survive, the problem is the pattern, not the cause.

leverage.detail: Before a big shared decision, write down what you need in a sentence or two and read it aloud. Ask your partner to do the same. Compare the two. This is the simplest test of whether you are both signing the same page.
Agree to revisit the arrangement in a month, as you would check a budget. “Let's look at this on the first Sunday” turns an assumption into a conversation you can both prepare for.

Try “If I stopped arranging this, what would happen?” The answer reveals whether the effort is shared or carried by one person. Ask it without accusation, then listen to the reply before deciding what to do next.

You can say no to a plan you did not help shape. “I do not want to sign on to this as it stands” is a complete sentence. A partner who hears that and adjusts is showing you how they handle your agency.

Note for your own clarity, not as a case file, the small promises kept and the ones that slipped. Patterns are easier to see on paper. If you decide to raise them, you can do it with specifics instead of a vague sense of unease.

closest.rationale: Martí drafted the Montecristi Manifesto and signed it with Máximo Gómez on 25 March 1895, so the text carried two signatures rather than one man's pledge alone.

cousin.tell: Unlike a broker tabling terms between two others, Martí drafted the Montecristi text and signed it himself alongside Gómez, rather than negotiating terms others would accept.

basis.observation: The Montecristi Manifesto was drafted by Martí and signed also by Máximo Gómez on 25 March 1895 in the Dominican town of Montecristi.

sections.identity: The Saint-Domingue revolutionary general who in mid-1794 left Spain for France after abolition was proclaimed, unlike loyalist allies Biassou and Papillon.

matches.why: Louverture left Georges Biassou and Jean-François Papillon's Spanish side in mid-1794 for the French once abolition was proclaimed, disagreeing with allies he had fought beside and standing by that reason.

pattern: When the French revolutionary government proclaimed abolition in mid-1794, Louverture changed sides, joining the French while his Spanish comrades Biassou and Papillon stayed loyal to Spain. The choice marked a public disagreement with allies he had fought beside. In everyday terms, it is the moment a person tells their own side where they differ and stands by the reason, even when the timing is awkward. That is a stance about a principle, not a template for how to treat a partner.

The constitution of 1801 named him governor for life, entrusting him with the colony's direction for the remainder of his life in recognition of his services. A role defined by duration can encourage people to treat arrangements as permanent. In a relationship, a similar dynamic appears when one person assumes the other will always be there and stops checking in. A title or a long history does not remove the need for regular, mutual agreement.

His cultivation regulations at Port-Républicain required managers, drivers and cultivators to perform their duties under threat of arrest and punishment, with negligent drivers reduced to simple cultivators. The rules tied compliance to consequences and demotion. Close relationships can drift toward a similar scorekeeping, where mistakes trigger penalties and status loss. Naming that pattern early, before it hardens, gives both people a chance to choose cooperation over punishment.

Police regulations issued in 1801 aimed to repress vice harmful to the colony and contrary to public order, conforming to earlier decrees. The language of public order can justify broad control. In private life, a partner who frames their preferences as necessary for harmony may be asking for obedience rather than agreement. The useful question is whether a rule protects both people or mainly shields one person from discomfort.

text: Listen for how your partner describes a past disagreement with their own friends or allies. Do they name the reason they differed, or do they only say the other side was difficult? A person who can state their own position plainly, without turning the other side into a villain, is showing you how they might handle a disagreement with you. You can ask, 'What did you want them to understand?'

Notice whether your partner treats a long-standing arrangement as permanent or as something to revisit. If they say, 'We've always done it this way,' you can reply, 'I'd like to check whether it still works for both of us.' The answer tells you whether they see agreements as shared choices or as fixed facts. You are listening for willingness to renegotiate, not for perfect agreement.
examples: In 1801 Toussaint Louverture was named governor for life of Saint-Domingue under the colony's new constitution, which entrusted him with its direction for the remainder of his life in recognition of his services during the revolution.

In mid-1794, after the French revolutionary government proclaimed the abolition of slavery, Toussaint Louverture left the Spanish for the French, while Georges Biassou and Jean-François Papillon remained loyal to Spain.

In 1801 Toussaint Louverture issued cultivation regulations at Port-Républicain, published in the Bulletin Officiel de Saint-Domingue, requiring managers, drivers and cultivators to perform their duties under threat of arrest and punishment, with negligent drivers reduced to simple cultivators.

In 1801, as governor of Saint-Domingue, Toussaint Louverture issued police regulations to repress vice harmful to the colony and contrary to public order, conforming to the police regulation of 20 Vendémiaire an IX and his proclamation of 19 Pluviôse.
